Using a neonatal mouse model of bacterial meningitis, we demonstrate that GBS infection significantly increases arachnoid barrier permeability, coinciding with alterations in Claudin-11 tight junction distribution and elevated meningeal production of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, CXCL1). CD206 + /Lyve1 + border-associated macrophages (BAMs) undergo significant morphological and molecular activation post-infection, but their depletion prior to GBS infection did not attenuate arachnoid barrier leakage or inflammatory cytokine levels during infection. We show that meningeal fibroblasts are a main source of proinflammatory cytokines in response to GBS infection and that exposure to the inflammatory cytokine TNF-α alone is sufficient to induce neonatal arachnoid barrier breakdown. These results support neonatal arachnoid barrier is vulnerable to cytokine-induced breakdown in bacterial infection and highlight the role of non-immune meningeal cells like fibroblasts during bacterial infection.

title: Aberrant recursive splicing in a human disease locus
abstract: Recursive splice sites are rare motifs postulated to facilitate splicing across massive introns and shape isoform diversity. The necessity of recursive splicing (RS) and its role in human disease are unsubstantiated. Here, we use CRISPR to model intronic deletions eliminating an RS site (RS1) in CADM2 and conferring risk for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and other neurobehavioral traits. Ablating RS1 in human induced neurons alters the gradient of RNA abundance across CADM2 's first intron, decreases CADM2 expression, and impacts transcript usage. Decreased CADM2 expression is reflected in reduced exon usage downstream of RS1 and global alteration to genes involved in neuronal processes. In vivo rodent models harboring Cadm2 RS1 deletions exhibit an attenuated effect on Cadm2 expression and modest changes in behavior and functional brain connectivity. This study demonstrates RS as a noncoding regulatory mechanism in a gene associated with a spectrum of neuropsychiatric and behavioral traits.

title: EpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics regulate nuclear deformation and promote gastric cancer metastasis
abstract: Diffuse gastric cancer is highly metastatic and lacks effective therapeutic targets. Using membrane proteomics, gastric cancer cell models, biophysical measurements, and in vivo metastasis assays, we identify EpCAM as a regulator of membrane-cytoskeletal mechanics. EpCAM overexpression was associated with reduced apparent plasma membrane tension, ERM-actin remodeling, increased traction forces, and nuclear deformation. Functional perturbation of ezrin and lamin A/C supported the involvement of membrane-cytoskeleton-nucleus mechanical coupling in confined migration. EpCAM knockout or monoclonal antibody blockade reduced tumor invasion and lymph node dissemination in vivo. These findings establish a mechanobiological framework linking EpCAM-dependent membrane mechanics to metastatic behavior and highlight EpCAM-associated mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in diffuse gastric cancer.

title: Pharmacologically targeting CDK12 induces BRCAness and synergizes with merestinib to exacerbate DNA damage in high-risk neuroblastoma
abstract: High-risk neuroblastoma remains a leading cause of pediatric cancer mortality, underscoring the need for novel therapeutics. MYCN amplification drives transcriptional addiction, creating vulnerabilities for therapeutic intervention. Inhibition of CDK12, a key regulator of transcription elongation, downregulates DNA damage response (DDR) genes. CDK12 inactivation using protein degraders and small molecules, including the orally bioavailable, selective CDK12/13 inhibitor OKI-1546, induced BRCAness and apoptosis in neuroblastoma cells. High-throughput compound screening combined with CDK12 inhibition/degradation revealed synergistic interactions encompassing multiple biological pathways. Merestinib, a multi-kinase inhibitor, emerged as the top synergistic agent across a panel of neuroblastoma in vitro models. Combining OKI-1546 with merestinib amplified DDR downregulation and diminished MYCN-driven signaling. OKI-1546 treatment reduced tumor growth and extended survival in vivo, which was enhanced when combined with merestinib. Whilst further in vivo validation is warranted, our findings nominate CDK12 as a promising therapeutic target in high-risk neuroblastoma, which can be exploited through combinatorial treatments.

title: Untranslated region rewiring defines a novel class of oncogene fusions
abstract: Gene fusions in cancer are traditionally understood to generate hybrid proteins with altered functions that promote malignancy. Here, we define a previously unrecognized class of oncogenic fusions that preserve protein structure but replace the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR), thereby rewiring translational regulation. Using the MET oncogene as a paradigm, we show that 5' UTR-replacing fusions, identified across >200,000 cancer samples, increase MET protein abundance 5- to 10-fold without corresponding changes in mRNA levels. The resulting receptor remains correctly localized, ligand-responsive, and active, thereby promoting cell survival and motility. These fusion transcripts are detected following irradiation, documenting UTR rewiring in a post-treatment context. Beyond MET, similar 5' UTR-replacing fusions occur in FGFR1, JAK2, and NTRK2, where partner-derived 5 'UTRs are associated with reduced regulatory complexity and enhanced protein output. Together, our findings establish UTR rewiring as an overlooked mechanism of oncogene overexpression with implications for cancer genome annotation and precision oncology.

title: Macrophage-induced ferritin expression protects pancreatic cancer cells from ferroptosis
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) drive pro-tumorigenic signaling but also promote lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, making ROS regulation critical during high oxidative stress stages of tumor progression, such as metastasis. Loss of the antioxidant TIGAR in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells raises ROS and enhances metastatic behavior but also sensitizes cells to ferroptosis. To understand how TIGAR-null cells survive to metastasize, we examine the role of macrophage infiltration, which is increased in TIGAR-null tumors. Co-culturing TIGAR-null PDAC cells with macrophages protects them from ferroptosis. The tumor cells induce macrophage IL-6 secretion, which leads to the activation of STAT3 and upregulation of the iron-sequestering protein ferritin (FTH1) in cancer cells. FTH1 depletion in TIGAR-null cells restores ferroptosis sensitivity and reduces lung metastasis. These results suggest that the outcome of increased ROS in tumors may depend on the activation of mechanisms that selectively prevent ferroptosis while preserving ROS-induced oncogenic signaling and metastasis-promoting pathways.

title: Cingulate thrombospondin 4 protects against neuropathic pain and comorbid anxiodepression via interaction with EAAT2
abstract: Patients with neuropathic pain frequently present with emotional disorders. Cellular plasticity within anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is considered as a key interface linking pain and emotion. However, mounting efforts have been devoted to elucidating intracellular mechanisms of plasticity, how extracellular alterations trigger intracellular changes remains elusive. Thrombospondin (THBS), a key component of extracellular matrix (ECM), is involved in various pathophysiological processes. Here, we show that THBS4 is downregulated in the ACC following peripheral neuropathy. Overexpressing cingulate THBS4 alleviates pain hypersensitivity and anxiodepression. Mechanistic analysis indicates that THBS4 maintains glutamate homeostasis via direct regulation of excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2) in astrocytic membrane, further stabilizing abnormal plasticity of pyramidal neurons and eventually producing analgesic, anxiolytic, and antidepressive effects. Taken together, we show THBS4-mediated neuron-astrocyte crosstalk as a key mechanism underlying neuropathic pain and comorbid anxiodepression. Recombinant THBS4 protein represents a promising therapeutic strategy for treatment of neuropathic pain and anxiodepression.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains poorly understood. We developed UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, which integrates dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combined it with RNA-seq to profile the effects of perturbations on enhancer activity and target gene expression. We applied this approach to a library of 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assessed the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (or TFs; ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1) with diverse regulatory roles. Across knockout lines, we identified responsive enhancers that were either repressed or induced, often through motifs such as the p53 family of TFs. Enhancer-gene mapping revealed TF-specific programs, including repression of Wnt/p53 targets with ATF2 or LEF1 loss, downregulation of the FIRRE locus with CTCF loss, and compensatory upregulation of RNA polymerase II regulators following FOXA1 depletion. A deep learning model trained on enhancer sequences recapitulated core principles of enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and the influence of flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to the neurodevelopmental disorder-associated 16p12.1 deletion identified responsive enhancers linked to genes involved in axon guidance, synaptic plasticity, and translational control, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics generalizable to genetic mutations.

title: Spatial distribution of blood-brain barrier membrane proteins is controlled by sorting motifs and physiological signals in vivo
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB), formed by brain endothelial cells (BECs), creates a safe and homeostatic environment for proper brain function. While BECs are extraordinarily thin, their luminal and abluminal plasma membranes face markedly different environments: the blood and brain parenchyma, respectively. How BBB membrane proteins are spatially distributed between these membranes and the factors regulating their localization are not clear. Here, we establish a method for measuring polarized protein sorting at the BBB in vivo. We characterize the distribution of transporters and receptors on the luminal and abluminal plasma membranes and identify protein-intrinsic motifs that control polarized sorting. Finally, we observe a change in membrane protein distribution that aligns with circadian rhythms, revealing an under-appreciated dimension of BBB dynamics. This method can be broadly used for evaluating membrane protein landscape changes during development and disease and for choosing optimal molecular targets for BBB-crossing therapeutics.

title: A systemic circadian nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) signal engages the unfolded protein response and adipogenesis via the prefoldin complex
abstract: Abstract Daily light–dark cycles impose predictable environmental fluctuations that require coordinated temporal regulation of cellular physiology. This coordination is mediated by the circadian clock, which operates as a network of tissue oscillators; however, the molecular signals that convey circadian information between organs remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify nicotinic acid riboside (NaR) as a circulating metabolite whose rhythmicity depends on the liver clock. In differentiating 3T3-L1 adipocytes, NaR engages unfolded protein response (UPR) gene programs and modulates adipogenic competence. Proteome-wide stability profiling implicates the prefoldin complex as a molecular target of NaR signaling, linking NaR exposure to altered proteostasis. Functionally, NaR-induced UPR signaling converges on the adipogenic transcription factor CEBPA, which is a central regulator of adipogenesis. Importantly, sustained NaR exposure suppresses adipocyte lipid deposition, whereas temporally restricted NaR stimulation enhances adipogenesis, indicating that NaR acts in a time-dependent manner. Together, these findings identify NaR as a liver clock–controlled circulating metabolite that couples systemic circadian metabolism to adipocyte proteostasis and differentiation, revealing a mechanism by which temporal metabolic signals shape tissue-specific physiological outcomes. Highlights The circadian clock is required for rhythmic regulation of circulating nicotinic acid riboside (NaR). The liver clock is sufficient to generate NaR rhythmicity. NaR engages the prefoldin complex to regulate unfolded protein response signaling and Cebpa expression. Time-dependent NaR exposure differentially regulates CEBPA levels and adipocyte lipid deposition.

title: Molecular mechanisms of promoter silencing by transcriptional readthrough
abstract: Transcriptional interference is the in cis suppression of one transcriptional process by another. To define the mechanisms by which transcriptional readthrough is converted into stable gene silencing, we develop a mouse cell line model of cobalamin C deficiency associated with MMACHC silencing (epi-cblC) by deleting the Prdx1 intron 5 splice acceptor, thereby inducing antisense transcription across Mmachc. Readthrough results in ectopic H3K36me3 deposition, de novo DNA methylation, and stable silencing of Mmachc. Through systematic perturbations of transcription and the H3K36 and DNA methylation machinery, we demonstrate that antisense transcription is the primary driver of repression, whereas H3K36me3 contributes directly to promoter silencing and is further required for the establishment of DNA methylation, which in turn confers long-term stability. Together, these findings define a hierarchical silencing cascade by which transcriptional readthrough establishes stable gene repression and demonstrate that transcription itself can direct local chromatin remodeling and changes in gene expression.

title: Anterior cingulate feedback facilitates rapid global context modulation in primary visual cortex
abstract: Context modulates sensory processing in the cerebral cortex by suppressing responses to expected stimuli and enhancing responses to unexpected ones. Recent proposals argue that early sensory areas such as primary visual cortex (V1) are shaped only by local context, including recent stimulus history, whereas modulation by global context, such as learned temporal structure, is present exclusively in higher cortical areas. This view is incompatible with predictive coding theories. To directly dissociate local and global contextual influences, we used a global/local oddball paradigm in which mice viewed five-item sequences. Across conditions, sequence structure was held constant while stimulus identity and predictability were selectively manipulated, allowing the isolation of response modulations due to local deviance, global expectation, and stimulus repetition independently. In the canonical sequence (AAAA-B), B is locally deviant but globally predictable. Using two-photon calcium imaging and LFP recordings in mouse V1, we found that global predictability abolished context modulation: responses to B were equivalent to those evoked by a random sequence control (e.g., CDEAB). This effect emerged rapidly, after only <10 sequence repetitions, demonstrating fast learning of global structure. When the stimulus was globally deviant, either by replacing B with a novel stimulus (AAAA-C) or by presenting B unpredictably in a standard oddball paradigm, V1 exhibited robust response enhancement. These effects required feedback from anterior cingulate area (ACa), establishing a causal role for higher cortical circuits in conveying global predictions to V1. Strikingly, when an additional A replaced B (AAAA-A), responses were strongly suppressed despite global deviance, indicating that stimulus-specific adaptation may constrain the expression of global prediction error signals in early sensory cortex.

title: Proprioceptive sensory-driven mechanisms shape Clarke’s column development
abstract: Coordinated locomotion depends not only on motor programs but also on the sensory feedback that refines them. Proprioceptive sensory neurons (pSNs) modulate motor circuits through direct synapses, yet their role in shaping spinal cord circuits has remained unclear. Here, we uncover an essential function for pSNs in organizing Clarke's column (CC) neurons, a major spinocerebellar population. Although CC neurons are born early in embryogenesis, their distinctive columnar architecture emerges postnatally and depends on direct pSN input. Genetic ablation of pSNs reduces the number of CC neurons and disrupts their somatic and dendritic organization. Blocking neurotransmission or eliminating Piezo2-dependent mechanotransduction produces overlapping defects, revealing that both the presence and activity of pSNs are required for CC maturation. RNA sequencing identifies a molecular signature of pSN-dependent regulation, implicating the axon guidance receptor Unc5c as a candidate regulator. Our findings reveal an unrecognized role for pSNs in spinal circuit development.

title: USP9X promotes the degradation of trapped translation factors on collided ribosomes
abstract: Various ribosome-associated quality control pathways safeguard translation fidelity by detecting and resolving aberrant translation events. Recently, a pathway that senses stalled ribosomes with an occluded A-site has been described. The small molecules NVS1.1 and ternatin-4 induce ribosome stalling by trapping eukaryotic release factor 1 (eRF1) and elongation factor 1A1 (eEF1A1), respectively, within the ribosomal A-site, thereby promoting their ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Additionally to the previously identified factors GCN1, RNF14, and RNF25, we identify here the deubiquitinase USP9X as a regulator of this pathway. In the absence of USP9X deubiquitinase activity, eRF1 is still ubiquitinated but fails to undergo efficient degradation. However, compared with wild-type cells, K6-linked ubiquitin chains accumulate on eRF1 in cells lacking USP9X activity, suggesting that USP9X trims K6-linked ubiquitin chains during a late step of substrate processing. Furthermore, clearance of trapped eRF1 engages a feedback mechanism involving 4EHP and the integrated stress response (ISR) to suppress translation, whereas impaired degradation prevents translational shutdown.

title: Human organ chip models recapitulate FRC-driven high endothelial venule differentiation, immune recruitment, and cancer-induced disruption
abstract: High endothelial venules (HEVs) are specialized post-capillary venules that gate lymphocyte entry into lymph nodes, yet human in vitro models that capture their specialization remain limited. Here, we develop a perfusable human HEV-on-chip in which blood endothelial cells (BECs) form an engineered microvessel within a collagen-fibrin matrix populated by human fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs). The presence of FRCs, without exogenous LIGHT, drives HEV-associated marker expression (PNAd/MECA-79 and VCAM-1) and a plump endothelial wall enwrapped by a thickened laminin + basement membrane, recapitulating features of lymph-node HEVs. Functionally, HEV-like vessels support markedly increased T-lymphocyte adhesion while preserving VE-cadherin junctions. Introducing MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells in an adjacent channel reduces MECA-79, disrupts junctional organization, and increases permeability without inducing apoptosis. Together, this platform defines a stromal instruction program for human HEV identity and a tractable model of cancer-associated HEV dysfunction.

title: Peptide signaling in the paraventricular thalamus is essential for disrupted adult reward behaviors consequent to early-life adversity
abstract: Abstract Early-life adversity (ELA) is strongly linked to emotional disorders characterized by dysregulated reward behaviors including diminished motivation for and enjoyment of rewards (anhedonia). However, how transient ELA leads to enduring disruptions of reward behaviors remains unclear. Using activity-dependent genetic labeling during ELA, we previously found that the paraventricular thalamic nucleus (PVT) uniquely distinguishes ELA from typical rearing, and inhibiting ELA-activated PVT cells in adult ELA mice rescued reward behaviors in a sex-specific manner. However, the cellular mechanisms by which ELA alters the function of PVT neurons enduringly, to impact adult reward behaviors is unresolved. Here, we probed potential gene expression mechanisms by assessing reward-induced gene translation selectively in early-life activated (TRAPed) PVT cells, and identified genes regulated by reward in a sex-specific way. Combining data- and hypothesis-driven approaches, we targeted the corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor type 1 (CRHR1) as potentially mediating ELA-induced disruptions of reward behaviors. We find that CRISPR-Cas9-mediated Crhr1 deletion in TRAPed-PVT cells restores typical reward behaviors in ELA mice. Our results provide insight into the developmental origin of mental illness and identify potentially powerful molecular targets for prevention or mitigation of the consequences of ELA on reward behaviors germane to human mental illness.

title: NONO mitigates transcription-replication conflicts during replication stress by restraining BRD4-dependent transcription elongation
abstract: Transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs) drive genomic instability and are linked to tumorigenesis and treatment response. Replication stress exacerbates TRCs, but how cells coordinate transcription and replication to limit these conflicts remains unclear. Here, we identify NONO as a key regulator that maintains transcription-replication balance via BRD4 under replication stress. Replication stress triggers NONO acetylation at K243, enhancing BRD4 binding. On single-stranded DNA, NONO-BRD4 form condensates that block paused RNA polymerase II (RNAP2) release, fine-tuning elongation. NONO loss causes aberrant accumulation of elongating RNAP2 at termination regions, promoting TRCs and genomic instability. Conditions that increase origin firing, including ATR inhibition or BRCA2 deficiency, further exacerbate this phenotype in NONO-deficient cells, leading to pronounced synthetic lethality. Together, these findings define a NONO-mediated surveillance mechanism that couples replication stress to transcriptional restraint via condensate-dependent regulation of BRD4, and identify NONO as a potential therapeutic target in replication stress-driven cancers.

title: Mitochondrial stress induces transcription of cytosolic and mitochondrial protein synthesis components via NHR-180
abstract: ), which promotes mitochondrial biogenesis and proteostasis, is regulated by the transcription factor ATFS-1. In C. elegans, impaired atfs-1 expression perturbs mitochondrial function and slows development. Here, using an RNAi suppressor screen, we find that inhibition of the nuclear hormone receptor NHR-180 increases mitochondrial function and developmental rate in atfs-1(null) worms. NHR-180 levels increase and become more nuclear-localized during mitochondrial dysfunction, inducing transcription of genes required for protein synthesis on cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomes. The NHR-180 ligand-binding domain interacts with AMP, suggesting that NHR-180 may link cellular energy status to protein synthesis during mitochondrial stress. However, NHR-180-dependent activity is associated with exacerbated mitochondrial dysfunction. Consistent with these findings, inhibition of the S6 kinase homolog RSKS-1 increases mitochondrial function in atfs-1(null) worms. S6 kinase inhibition also increases respiration and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content in mammalian ATF5-knockout cells and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-deficient models.

title: Lipid droplet targeting drives substrate access during very long chain fatty acid activation by Fat1
abstract: Fatty acids require conjugation with coenzyme A (CoA) for their incorporation into membrane lipids. Of these, very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), the precursors of yeast ceramides, are particularly hydrophobic. Yet, it remains unresolved where and how the sole VLCFA-CoA synthetase Fat1 activates them. Here, we show that lipid droplets (LDs) are both the site of free VLCFA storage and their place of activation. Free VLCFAs preferentially partition into LDs in molecular simulations and in vitro reconstitutions, whereas Fat1 targets the LD surface in cells via an N-terminal amphipathic helix. Structural predictions identify an essential hydrophobic cavity in Fat1 that connects the active site to the membrane, suggesting that VLCFAs shuttle directly from the LD core into the enzymatic pocket. Our model explains how the organelle targeting of a fatty acid activator evolved to match the biophysical properties, and consequently, the subcellular localization of its highly hydrophobic substrate.

title: The NuRD complex shapes RNA polymerase III activity at highly expressed tRNA gene clusters, tuning the dynamic range of cellular tRNA pools
abstract: RNA polymerase III (Pol III) produces noncoding RNAs involved in diverse cellular activities, including translation (tRNA, 5S rRNA, 7SL RNA), RNA processing (U6 snRNA, RPPH1, RMRP), and transcription regulation (7SK snRNA). In this way, Pol III activity must be broadly coupled with cellular demands for protein accumulation and growth, increasing in response to nutrient availability and decreasing during differentiation and exit from proliferation. However, the currently established mechanisms of Pol III regulation remain relatively limited, due in part to the few Pol III-centered protein-protein interaction (PPI) studies performed to date. To address this gap, we first investigated PPIs shared by multiple Pol III subunits to understand the macromolecular interactome of Pol III, with special attention directed at potential regulatory candidates. Our proteomic survey uncovers interactions between Pol III and the NuRD (Nucleosome Remodeling and Deacetylase) complex. Taken further, we show that NuRD localizes to active Pol III-transcribed genes and that its recruitment is Pol III-dependent but nonrandom, with peak occupancy and regulatory hallmarks converging on tRNA gene clusters associated with notably high expression levels. Inhibiting NuRD-associated histone deacetylase function reduces Pol III transcription at these sites, suggesting NuRD restricts Pol III and thereby modulates the global dynamic range of Pol III-derived RNA species. These findings are congruent with the transcriptionally repressive nature of NuRD and bring-to-light a new regulatory mechanism that may couple signaling events and changes in metabolic needs with the dynamic availability of specific tRNA pools.

title: Inhibiting the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex selectively enhances unsupervised statistical learning
abstract: Abstract The brain must balance the automatic extraction of environmental regularities with top-down cognitive control, yet the causal neural mechanisms governing this interplay are debated. In particular, the hemispheric contributions of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) remain unresolved. Here, we applied inhibitory repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) to the left, right, or bilateral DLPFC in 95 healthy adults during a probabilistic sequence learning task. We found that inhibiting the right and bilateral DLPFC significantly enhanced statistical learning compared to sham stimulation, while the left DLPFC stimulation group remained similar to sham. Contrary to the hypothesis that this competition is mediated by the suppression of existing knowledge, episodic memory performance was unaffected across all stimulation groups. These findings challenge a direct episodic gating mechanism and suggest the DLPFC’s influence on statistical learning is hemisphere-dependent. As an alternative, we propose that right DLPFC inhibition shifts cognitive processing toward a more exploratory information-sampling strategy, a view supported by our finding of significantly greater reaction time variability in the right and bilateral stimulation groups. Together, our results provide causal evidence for a right-lateralized suppressive influence of the DLPFC on unsupervised learning and suggest its modulatory role is linked to information processing style rather than direct competition with episodic memory systems.

title: Deciphering genomic adaptations and climate resilience in the intertidal seagrass Zostera japonica
abstract: Seagrasses are coastal foundation species that support ecosystem stability but face increasing global change. Here, we assemble a chromosome-level reference genome for the intertidal seagrass Zostera japonica to investigate adaptive evolution and climate resilience. Comparative genomic analyses reveal features underlying intertidal adaptation, including ion transport, circadian regulation, and stress responses. We identify positively selected genes associated with the transition to marine environments. Population genomic analyses identify strong divergence between northern and southern populations, reflecting deep historical separation, largely independent evolutionary trajectories, and local adaptation. Selection signals are enriched in stress response and ion transport genes, among which TIP3-1 confers tolerance to both salinity and heat. Genomic offset projections indicate greater climate vulnerability in northern populations, whereas southern populations show higher adaptive potential and may serve as genetic sources for assisted gene flow. Together, our study provides a genomic framework for understanding adaptation and guiding conservation under climate change.

title: TDP2-mediated DNA repair regulates the dynamics of neuronal early response gene transcription and cortical neuron connectivity
abstract: Neuronal activity induces topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4, and facilitates rapid ERG transcription. However, the mechanisms that repair activity-induced DSBs and their significance for neuronal function remain ill-defined. Here, we report that depletion of tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2) in cultured mouse cortical neurons delays the repair of TOP2B-mediated DSBs and prolongs ERG expression following neuronal stimulation. Deleting Tdp2 in excitatory forebrain neurons in vivo caused DSB accrual, ERG overexpression, and increased excitatory synaptic transmission and cortical circuit dysfunction. Whereas proliferating cells utilize alternative pathways to process TOP2B-mediated DSBs, we find that such mechanisms are relatively inactive in postmitotic neurons. Overall, these results indicate that TDP2-mediated DNA repair is crucial for the temporal control of ERG transcription and suggest that defective repair of activity-induced DSBs could underlie neurological abnormalities in individuals with TDP2 mutations.

title: TM6SF2 acts at ER membrane contact sites to enable RAB7-dependent endolysosomal VLDL secretion and maintain Golgi structure
abstract: Although a loss-of-function variant of TM6SF2 is a highly penetrant risk factor for steatotic liver disease, including progression to cirrhosis and cancer, its normal function is largely unknown. Here we show that endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized TM6SF2 forms membrane contact sites (MCSs) with late endosomes/lysosomes, where it activates the small GTPase RAB7 to enable an endolysosomal route for selective secretion of lipid-rich very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) particles. In accord, TM6SF2 and RAB7 deficiency similarly cause endolysosomal VLDL retention and accumulation of enlarged late endosomes/lysosomes. TM6SF2 further binds to VAMP-associated protein (VAP) ER-anchor proteins to maintain MCSs between the ER, endosomes, and the trans-Golgi network, with TM6SF2 deficiency causing Golgi fragmentation and disruption of cGAS-STING signaling known to prevent cirrhosis and cancer by clearing senescent hepatocytes. Our findings establish TM6SF2 as an ER-MCS component that enables endolysosomal VLDL secretion and maintains Golgi structure, which suggests that TM6SF2 loss of function causes liver disease through steatosis-dependent and independent mechanisms.

title: Structural basis for cross-alphaherpesvirus neutralization by an antibody targeting a conserved hotspot on glycoprotein B
abstract: Alphaherpesviruses, including herpes simplex viruses (HSV-1/2) and pseudorabies virus (PRV), pose significant threats to human and animal health, yet broad-spectrum interventions remain elusive. Here, we characterize C12A6, a neutralizing antibody (nAb) targeting glycoprotein B (gB) that cross-neutralizes HSV-1, HSV-2, and PRV and confers substantial, although incomplete, therapeutic protection against lethal HSV-1 or PRV infection. Cryo-electron microscopy structures of C12A6 in complex with PRV gB and HSV-2 gB reveal that the antibody engages a conserved conformational epitope on Domain I (DI). A conserved interaction framework, anchored by invariant polar contacts and a hydrophobic core, supports recognition across divergent alphaherpesvirus gBs. Comparison with the broader alphaherpesvirus antibody 16F9 shows that C12A6 additionally engages less-conserved peripheral residues, providing a structural basis for its more restricted recognition breadth. These findings define the structural basis for C12A6-mediated cross-neutralization and illuminate the functional architecture of gB DI as a target for broad-spectrum antiviral development.

title: Genome architecture shapes transcriptional responses to topoisomerase depletion in C. elegans
abstract: DNA supercoiling is an intrinsic consequence of transcription that must be resolved to maintain proper gene expression. How supercoiling shapes transcription dynamics in animal genomes remains unclear. Here, we acutely depleted topoisomerases in Caenorhabditis elegans and applied nascent transcription profiling, nuclear RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), histone modification mapping, and long-read sequencing to capture the transcriptional and chromatin responses to topological stress. We find that topoisomerase depletion preferentially inhibits and uncouples expression of convergent genes, while transcription initiation and coordinated expression of divergent genes are comparatively maintained. Topoisomerase degradation hinders transcription elongation globally, resulting in reduced production of longer transcripts and overall shortening of poly(A) tails. These elongation defects are not accompanied by global changes in elongation-associated histone modifications but coincide with modest reductions in promoter and enhancer marks. Our results indicate that genome architecture shapes transcriptional responses to DNA supercoiling, uncovering a topological basis for coordinated gene expression in a multicellular organism.

title: Histone H3K27 methylation states are sequentially catalyzed in cycling cells
abstract: Polycomb domains form at silenced genes and are marked by histone H3 lysine 27 tri-methylation, but it is unclear how this methylation is maintained following DNA replication in proliferating cells. Here, we use CUT&Tag chromatin profiling to track the dynamics of H3K27 methylation in human cells. We find that tri-methylation in Polycomb domains is maintained by stepwise methylation after DNA replication. Outside of Polycomb domains, thousands of transcriptionally inactive genes gain histone H3K27 di-methylation hours after DNA replication. Acute treatment with small-molecule inhibitors of the Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) histone methyltransferase slows H3K27 methylation during S-phase of the cell cycle and increases acetylation of the residue. This effect is most pronounced at Polycomb domains replicating in early S-phase, thereby suggesting that early replication and slow histone methylation confer plasticity to developmentally silenced genes. Together, our results explain how H3K27 modification patterns are faithfully duplicated in rapidly proliferating cells.

title: ICAM-1 functions as a functional receptor for encephalomyocarditis virus and reveals a compensatory interplay with ICAM-4
abstract: Encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) is the most widespread zoonotic pathogen that causes piglet death. EMCV enters cells via caveolin-mediated endocytosis. However, the receptors required for EMCV entry into the cells are unknown. Here, we show that intercellular cell adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) serves as a significant functional receptor during adsorption and entry. ICAM-1 binds directly to the EMCV viral proteins VP1 and VP2 with high affinity. Consistently, a soluble ICAM-1 fusion protein or anti-ICAM-1 blocking antibody impairs EMCV infection in susceptible human and mouse cells. Domain 1 of ICAM-1 is involved in the recognition of EMCV. ICAM-4 serves as a receptor in ICAM-1 knockout/knockdown mice and cell lines during EMCV infection. These findings suggest that ICAM-1 and ICAM-4 are entry receptors for EMCV and that targeting ICAM-1 D1 could be a potential strategy for the development of antivirals against EMCV.

title: Ataxin-2 downregulation rewires neuronal and astrocytic metabolism to protect against TDP-43 toxicity
abstract: Abstract Ataxin-2 (ATXN2) is a genetic modifier of TDP-43 toxicity and a promising therapeutic target in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, the mechanisms underlying its neuroprotective effects remain poorly understood. Here we show that ataxin-2 reduction confers neuroprotection by engaging adaptive metabolic programs in both neuronal and glial cells. Using global proteomic profiling in yeast and mouse TDP-43 models, we establish that pbp1/ataxin-2 (pbp1 is the yeast ataxin-2 ortholog) activates orthogonal stress-adaptive programs that enable alternative energy production and augment trophic support, rather than simply reversing TDP-43-induced damage. In neurons, ataxin-2 downregulation activates glycolysis and reductive glutamine carboxylation driven by IDH1, restoring ATP production independently of impaired mitochondria. In astrocytes, ataxin-2 downregulation upregulates cholesterol biosynthesis via HMGCS1, enhancing trophic support to neurons in a non-cell-autonomous manner. Full neuroprotection requires both mechanisms: neuronal survival is only completely rescued when ataxin-2 is reduced in the context of neuron-astrocyte co-cultures. Importantly, ataxin-2 downregulation protects against both TDP-43 gain-of-function and loss-of-function toxicity, broadening its therapeutic relevance. Collectively, our findings reveal novel mechanisms by which ataxin-2 orchestrates adaptive metabolic resilience and establish ataxin-2 as a regulator of stress-adaptive response in brain cells under the conditions of stress.

title: Single-cell analyses reveal lymph node-tumor ecosystem remodeling during lymph node metastasis of gastric cancer
abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) is a highly aggressive malignancy with a strong propensity for lymph node metastasis. To characterize the metastatic ecosystem, we perform integrated single-cell transcriptomic and T cell receptor profiling of 156,871 cells from 30 primary tumors and matched sentinel lymph nodes (SLNs), spanning non-metastatic and metastatic tumors and SLNs from non-metastatic to micro- and macro-metastatic states. We identify LN-enriched progenitor exhausted T cells as a potential reservoir for tumor-infiltrating exhausted CD8 + T cells and reveal dynamic remodeling of the lymph node microenvironment by tumor-associated macrophages during disease progression. We further show that ILC3s promote a pro-metastatic microenvironment in micro-metastatic lymph nodes through the AREG-EGFR axis, facilitating lymphatic dissemination and subsequent establishment of CD24 + tumor cells. Collectively, these findings provide a stage-resolved view of the tumor-lymph node metastatic ecosystem and identify potential therapeutic targets in GC.

title: Neoplastic and non-neoplastic astrocyte states converge on mesenchymal and injury-response programs during glioblastoma recurrence
abstract: Glioblastomas initially respond to radiotherapy but invariably recur, often within high-dose radiation treatment fields. Although stromal radiation responses are incompletely understood, evidence suggests that the tumor microenvironment becomes tumor-supportive after therapy. Using a genetically engineered glioblastoma mouse model, we profiled healthy brain, primary tumors, and post-radiotherapy recurrences with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and immunofluorescence. Across 13 non-neoplastic cell types and 10 tumor cell states, we mapped transcriptional adaptations accompanying progression from healthy brain to primary and recurrent glioblastoma. We find distinct astrocyte states linked to disease stage, including reactive, non-neoplastic astrocytes and tumor cells adopting reactive astrocyte-like phenotypes. Reactive astrocyte-like tumor cells with mesenchymal and injury-response signatures are enriched after radiotherapy and persist in recurrent tumors. Receptor-ligand interactions between reactive astrocytes and tumor cells include known and putative drivers of aggressiveness. These findings highlight convergent reactive astrocyte programs in astrocytes and tumor cells as potential mediators of glioblastoma radioresistance.

title: Lymphangiogenesis driven by VEGF-C reshapes tumor immune landscape and enables tumor eradication by viral immunotherapy in mouse melanoma models
abstract: ABSTRACT Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor C (VEGF-C) is a key lymphangiogenic growth factor expressed by many types of cancer. Here, we investigated the effects of tumor-derived VEGF-C on the therapeutic efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy with avian paramyxoviruses APMV-1 (NDV) and AMPV-4. Treatment of B16F10 tumors not expressing VEGF-C with either virus led to tumor growth delay, and complete responses were rare. In contrast, when tumors expressed VEGF-C, viral therapy led to complete remission and long-term immunological memory in most mice. Upon re-challenge, most mice remained tumor- and metastasis-free for over 18 months, indicating durable immunity. VEGF-C induced tumor lymphangiogenesis, which correlated with high CD8 + and CD4 + T-cell densities in proximity of lymphatic vessels. Spectral flow cytometry revealed distinct changes in the composition and activation of CD8 + , CD4 + T cells and NK cells associated with complete remission. In responders, tumors were highly enriched in CD8 + CD25 + PD-1 + effector T cells. Composition of T cells was altered in sentinel and in contralateral lymph nodes, indicating a systemic immune response. Taken together, these data demonstrate VEGF-C-induced changes in tumor immune landscape which are critical for achieving complete response and support combining VEGF-C with APMV virotherapy as a novel highly effective strategy for cancer treatment.

title: NAD+ precursor treatment prevents cardiomyopathy but disrupts erythroid maturation in mitochondrial progeria
Early-life high-fat diet accelerates the development of vagal satiation signaling and predisposes females to overconsumption
abstract: Overconsumption of foods rich in fats, sugars, and calories is a major contributing factor to increased risk for cardiometabolic disease. Ingestive experience with these foods can begin early in children, yet there is limited understanding of the impact of early life nutrition on the development of vagal afferent neurons necessary for coordinating appetitive and satiating behaviors. To this end, mice reared on a chow diet (control) were compared to those reared on a high-fat diet (HFDEARLY). We demonstrate that the vagally-mediated satiation response to cholecystokinin (CCK) does not mature until adolescence in chow-reared mice. However, HFDEARLY exposure triggers a precocious maturation of this response, accompanied by transcriptomic changes in the nodose ganglion. Durable changes in appetitive behaviors were also evident in adult HFDEARLY mice, which consumed more lipid than control mice. Behavioral analyses point to alterations in orosensory integration and enhanced appetition in adult HFDEARLY mice, establishing nutrient exposure as a significant contributor to vagal circuit maturation and function.

title: Divergent interplay between STIM1 and STIM2 sets the efficacy of central synapses
abstract: Stromal interaction molecules (STIMs) are endoplasmic reticulum resident calcium (Ca 2+ sensors that modulate Ca 2+ homeostasis. Mammals express two isoforms, STIM1 and STIM2, but whether they serve redundant or distinct roles in neurotransmission remains poorly defined. Using Ca 2+ imaging and electrophysiology in hippocampal neurons lacking STIM1, STIM2, or both, we examined presynaptic and postsynaptic functions of STIMs at excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Both isoforms redundantly activated store-operated Ca 2+ entry and amplified presynaptic Ca 2+ influx, sustaining neurotransmitter release by expanding the readily releasable pool of synaptic vesicles and accelerating vesicle replenishment. These presynaptic roles were synapse specific: STIM1 predominantly supported excitatory synapses, whereas STIM2 was critical for the inhibitory counterparts. Postsynaptically, STIM1 and STIM2 exerted opposing effects on glutamate and GABA receptor levels, such that simultaneous loss of both isoforms rescued postsynaptic function. Together, the findings show that STIM1 and STIM2 differentially tune synaptic efficacy according to synapse type and subcellular compartment.

title: The COX2-PGE2-PKA axis suppresses antiviral immunity by inhibiting mtDNA-dependent STING activation
abstract: SUMMARY The innate immune cGAS-STING pathway is activated by cytosolic double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) to induce type I interferon (IFN) response, which is essential for mounting the antiviral response. However, STING activation during viral infection is often insufficient to achieve complete viral clearance, suggesting the existence of additional mechanisms that evade its activity. Here, we identified COX2/PGE 2 as a negative regulator of STING activation, particularly in response to arising cytosolic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) generated during HSV-1 infection. Mechanistically, PGE 2 , through the EP4-cAMP-PKA axis, induces mitophagy to remove defective mitochondria and hence prevent the accumulation of immunostimulatory cytosolic mtDNA, thereby dampening STING-mediated type I IFN and antiviral response. Furthermore, we identified STOML2 as a downstream target of PKA that connects mitochondrial quality control with the regulation of innate immune signaling. Together, our findings establish the COX2/PGE 2 /PKA axis as a negative regulator of mtDNA-STING signaling that may be targeted to potentiate STING-mediated type I IFN and innate immunity. Abstract Figure Graphical abstract

title: Cross-species atlas of bacterial RNA 3′ ends reveals termination mechanistic signatures and evolutionary patterns
abstract: Deciphering the generation mechanisms and regulatory roles of bacterial transcript 3' termini requires large-scale 3' terminus data. We repurpose PATHOgenex, an available RNAtag-seq dataset, leveraging RNAtag-seq-specific read patterns associated with 3' termini to generate the "Bacterminome" atlas, a rich resource of species- and condition-dependent transcript 3' termini of 32 bacterial human pathogens grown under 10-12 conditions. Analysis of sequence elements near 3' termini revealed, along with the classical intrinsic terminator, other known and newly detected signatures, highlighting the wealth of termination-associated sequence elements. Intriguingly, orthologous genes with corresponding 3' termini show different termination mechanisms in different bacteria, often matching the dominant mechanism of the respective bacterial species. Analysis of condition-dependent 3' termini revealed some conservation across species, supporting the conjecture that alternative 3' termini can play a role in gene expression regulation. Our resource, available through a user-friendly web server (https://bacterminome.huji.ac.il), provides a platform for studying transcription termination at an unprecedented scope.

title: Molecular triage and isoform protection safeguard ubiquitin chain editing on DNA
abstract: In an accompanying study, we identify the RPA-ZUP1 complex as a ubiquitin chain-editing machine that promotes removal of RPA from ssDNA. Because loss of ZUP1 causes pathological RPA trapping on ssDNA, cells must preserve a functional RPA-ZUP1 pool to sustain RPA turnover. How this homeostasis is achieved is unknown. Here, we show that ZUP1 is subject to ubiquitin-dependent fate control. ZUP1 ubiquitination promotes recruitment of p97/VCP and ATXN3, defining a molecular triage pathway that protects ZUP1 from premature proteasomal degradation. Opposing this, the E3 ligases UBR5 and HUWE1 define a degradative branch that limits ZUP1 abundance, with HUWE1 restricting its accumulation on damaged chromatin. We further show that cells express a naturally occurring ZUP1 isoform resistant to efficient ubiquitination and turnover, suggesting that isoform diversity provides a protected pool of chain-editing activity. Together, these findings define a homeostatic system that preserves ZUP1 while limiting its persistence on damaged chromatin.

title: Sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation delineates a progression toward the totipotent-like state
abstract: The in vitro induction of 8-cell-like cells (8CLCs) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provides a model to study the regulatory principles of totipotency and zygotic genome activation (ZGA). However, the cellular dynamics underlying 8CLC emergence remain poorly understood. Here, we generate a TPRX1-EGFP/HERVL-tdTomato dual-reporter hPSC line to resolve the stepwise acquisition of totipotent-like identity. We show that 8CLC induction follows an ordered trajectory in which TPRX1 activation precedes the emergence of TPRX1 + HERVL + cells, which most closely resemble the in vivo 8-cell embryo transcriptionally. Single-cell transcriptomics and time-resolved flow cytometry further define a continuous transition from the primed state through a TPRX1 + intermediate to the HERVL + 8CLC state. CRISPRi and RNA-directed perturbations support functional contributions of HERVL elements and HERVL-derived RNA to this transition, while potential locus-dependent mechanisms remain unresolved. Together, these findings establish sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation as a defining feature of human 8CLC induction.

title: The conserved NUS-1/DHDDS-1 complex links N-glycosylation to lipid and lysosomal homeostasis in C. elegans
abstract: N-glycosylation is essential for proteome integrity, yet the systemic roles of the cis-prenyltransferase (cis-PT) complex remain poorly defined. Using Caenorhabditis elegans, we demonstrate that this complex is a dual regulator of global lipid and lysosomal homeostasis. Mechanistically, NUS-1 physically associates with the core oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) complex to coordinate N-glycan transfer. Loss of NUS-1/DHDDS-1 triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, lysosomal collapse, and systemic lipopenia. This lipid defect arises from impaired N-glycosylation of the SREBP cleavage-activating protein (SCAP). cis-PT deficiency causes unglycosylated SCAP to undergo massive degradation and absolute physical entrapment within the ER, preventing SREBP nuclear translocation and downstream lipid synthesis. Furthermore, pathogenic mutations cause dysfunction through distinct molecular mechanisms: pocket integrity disruption or catalytic impairment. These findings uncover an essential crosstalk between protein glycosylation and global lipid metabolism, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the systemic pathophysiology of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG).

title: RUNX1-ETO oncoprotein levels determine the balance between endothelial reprogramming and pre-leukemic growth in a human ES cell model of AML
abstract: In t(8;21) acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the RUNX1 DNA binding domain is fused to RUNX1T1 (ETO) producing the RUNX1-ETO fusion protein. We previously showed that t(8;21) leukemic stem cells aberrantly activate endothelial signaling pathways to initiate blast cell proliferation. Here, we employed a human embryonic stem cell (ESC) line carrying an inducible RUNX1-ETO transgene to determine whether endothelial signaling pathway activation depends on disease progression or is directly induced by RUNX1-ETO. Single-cell analyses demonstrate that RUNX1-ETO reprograms ESC-derived myeloid progenitors towards endothelial cells. We show (1) that endothelial reprogramming is RUNX1-ETO concentration-dependent and irreversible, (2) at similar RUNX1-ETO and RUNX1 expression levels, a sub-population of blood progenitors can escape reprogramming, and (3) keeps proliferating when co-cultured with endothelial cells. Our experiments highlight the role of cellular interactions in the maintenance of pre-leukemic cells and provide important insights into the earliest stages of genomic reprogramming by oncogenic transcription factors.

title: The lysis mechanism of the haloarchaeal virus HFTV1
abstract: Tailed bacteriophages can lyse their host with help of the holin-endolysin system. However, for archaeal tailed viruses (arTVs), whose archaeal hosts have a fundamentally different cell envelope, lysis mechanisms are unknown. In this study, we use the model archaeal virus-host system: Haloferax tailed virus 1 (HFTV1), which infects the methanobacteriote Haloferax gibbonsii LR2-5. We identified and characterized the lysis protein GP33, a small membrane protein that has no sequence homology with bacterial holins. Overexpression resulted in cell lysis, and the protein forms foci near the cell envelope. Molecular dynamics simulation suggests that it forms pores from which the lipids are repelled, which might result in cell lysis. Indeed, atomic force microscopy (AFM) showed that GP33 forms pores in membranes, which lead to complete membrane disruption at higher concentrations. With this work, we gain insight into a lysis mechanism from a tailed archaeal virus at the molecular level.

title: Polycystin-2 functions as a calcium leak channel under endoplasmic reticulum stress to protect against myocardial ischemia
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with autosomal polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) have an increased risk and worsened outcomes for acute myocardial infarction (AMI), but the mechanism behind this is unknown. Polycystin 2 (PC2), the protein encoded by one of the two main genes mutated in ADPKD, is a calcium-permeant channel ubiquitously expressed; however, its role in cardiomyocytes remains poorly understood. One hallmark of AMI is ER stress, which PC2 is known to regulate adaptively; however, whether PC2 regulates ER stress in the ischemic heart is unknown. Objective This study investigates the mechanism by which PC2 regulates ER stress in myocardial ischemia. Methods and Results PC2 protein was increased in human ischemic heart failure samples and murine myocardial infarct samples, and it was enriched at ER-mitochondrial contact sites. Induction of myocardial infarction (MI) in cardiomyocyte-specific PC2-KO mice led to cardiac dysfunction and reduced PERK expression compared to control MI mice. ER stress induced by tunicamycin in vitro blunted PERK phosphorylation and subsequent CHOP upregulation in PC2 KO cells. Tunicamycin-induced ER stress resulted in a PC2-dependent ER calcium leak and mitochondrial calcium transients, along with increased mitochondrial function, all of which were decreased in PC2 KO cells. Moreover, PC2 KO cells after ER stress exhibited decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased apoptosis. Isolated WT cardiomyocytes exhibited increased diastolic calcium after acute ER stress induction and increased mitochondrial uptake, neither of which was seen in PC2 KO cells. Re-expression of full-length PC2 in vitro restored both the calcium leak and PERK phosphorylation in PC2 KO cells under ER stress, but not a pathological mutant PC2 D511V, which impairs ion channel activity. Conclusions PC2 is upregulated during ER stress, where it localizes at ER-mitochondrial contact sites and acts as an ER calcium leak channel, thereby restoring cellular homeostasis during the adaptive phase of ER stress. PC2 provides cardioprotection during ischemic events by preventing maladaptive ER stress, which contributes to cardiac dysfunction. Graphical abstract

title: METTL4 interacts with histone methylation readers MRG1/2 to regulate alternative splicing and promote thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) functions in thermomorphogenesis, but how AS is regulated during this process remains unclear. Here we show that METTL4 physically interacts with MRG1/2 in Arabidopsis thaliana. The mettl4-1, mrg1 mrg2, and mettl4 mrg1 mrg2 mutants exhibit reduced hypocotyl elongation under warm temperature conditions (28°C), indicating that METTL4 and MRG1/2 cooperatively promote thermomorphogenesis. Transcriptome analysis revealed that both METTL4 and MRG1/2 are required for warm temperature-induced reprogramming of gene transcription and AS. Further analysis showed that METTL4 and MRG1/2 modulate the AS of key brassinosteroid (BR)-signaling genes BES1, GSK1, and SBI1 in thermomorphogenesis. In addition, METTL4 promotes MRG2 binding to the chromatin of BES1 and GSK1 loci. METTL4 also promotes hypocotyl elongation and regulates the AS of BR signaling genes independently of its methyltransferase activity. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that METTL4 and MRG1/2 co-regulate AS and BR signaling to promote thermomorphogenesis in Arabidopsis.

title: The TCF-1-E-protein axis preserves stem-like Th17 identity and prevents autoimmune pathology
abstract: T helper 17 (Th17) cells exhibit plasticity, transitioning from homeostatic cells to pathogenic effectors in autoimmune diseases. Although TCF-1 restrains Th17 pathogenicity by binding RORγt, mechanisms sustaining TCF-1 expression in mature Th17 cells and the transcriptional architecture governing the switch between states remain unknown. Using an interleukin 17 (IL-17) fate-mapping system deleting Tcf7 in cells with IL-17 history, we show that TCF-1 maintains homeostatic Th17 identity. TCF-1 deficiency does not impair Th17 generation but destabilizes the non-pathogenic state, causing loss of stem-like markers (SLAMF6 and CD27), acquisition of pathogenic features (CXCR6, T-bet, and IFN-γ), and exacerbated experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. Mechanistically, TCF-1 and E-proteins form a reciprocal feedback loop establishing a self-reinforcing transcriptional circuit; disruption of either collapses this circuit and unleashes pathogenicity. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals that TCF-1 downregulation is an early event in pathogenic conversion. Thus, the TCF-1-E-protein axis sustains TCF-1 expression and prevents pathogenic conversion.

title: SMURFs regulate mesendoderm differentiation through SMAD2-dependent ubiquitination of CDK9
abstract: Precise control of transcriptional timing is essential during embryonic development, where dynamic gene expression programs govern lineage specification. Promoter-proximal pausing of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and its regulated release into productive elongation constitute a critical checkpoint in transcriptional regulation. Nodal, a transforming growth factor β (TGF-β) family morphogen, promotes mesendoderm differentiation through SMAD2-dependent transcription, in part by promoting cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9)-mediated release of paused Pol II. While mechanisms of transcriptional activation downstream of Nodal are well characterized, how this transcriptional program is attenuated during gastrulation remains unclear. Here, we show that E3 ubiquitin ligases SMAD Ubiquitination Regulatory Factor (SMURF) 1 and SMURF2 are critical regulators of SMAD2-driven transcription. SMURF1/2 ubiquitinate CDK9 and promote its proteasome-mediated degradation, thereby restraining CDK9-dependent promoter-proximal pause release and productive transcription of SMAD2-dependent genes. Loss of SMURF function stabilizes CDK9, increases its occupancy at SMAD2 target genes, and enhances Pol II pause release, thereby sustaining mesendodermal gene expression. These findings reveal a ubiquitin-dependent mechanism that restricts morphogen-induced gene expression and ensures timely developmental progression.

title: An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease
abstract: Early diagnosis and timely treatment of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are critical to limit disease progression, yet integrated diagnostic-therapeutic strategies remain limited. Here, we design a synthetic probiotic system that responds to reactive oxygen species (ROS) to enable noninvasive detection of intestinal inflammation. We further engineer EcN-IL22, a therapeutic strain that conditionally expresses interleukin 22-fragment crystallizable (IL-22-Fc) fusion protein in situ to mitigate colitis-associated tissue damage. Mechanistically, EcN-IL22 activates epithelial IL-22 receptor 1/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (IL-22R1/STAT3) signaling, promoting epithelial barrier restoration and intestinal stem cell proliferation. We identify thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 13 (Trip13) and fidgetin-like 1 (Fignl1) as IL-22R1-responsive candidate genes associated with epithelial repair. Importantly, replacing the diagnostic output of the ROS-responsive circuit with IL-22-Fc enables inflammation-triggered therapeutic delivery and significantly alleviates colitis. Finally, EcN-IL22 demonstrates robust protective efficacy in a piglet colitis model, supporting its translational potential. Together, this work establishes an integrated probiotic platform for IBD diagnosis and regenerative therapy.

title: A MADS51 allele is associated with flowering-time divergence and contributes to ecological adaptation during wild rice speciation
abstract: Flowering-time divergence can contribute to ecological speciation, but causal genes and mutations remain largely unknown in wild plants. Here, we investigate flowering-time divergence between the wild rice species Oryza rufipogon and O. nivara. By establishing a transformation system for wild rice and combining genome scans, population genomics, and functional assays, we identify MADS51 as a contributor to flowering-time divergence. Knockout of MADS51 in O. rufipogon accelerates flowering, whereas overexpression delays flowering. A functional haplotype (functional haplotype 2 [FH2]), defined by three nonsynonymous substitutions and a 4-bp frameshift, is nearly fixed in Southeast Asian O. nivara. Complementation assays confirm that FH2 promotes earlier flowering than ancestral haplotypes. Population genetic analyses reveal a selective sweep associated with FH2, which appears to have arisen de novo in O. nivara. These findings provide insights into how de novo mutation can contribute to phenotypic differentiation in wild rice.

title: Multi-omics profiling of the choroid plexus reveals developmental cellular remodeling, early immune gene activation, and epithelial cell heterogeneity
abstract: Brain development and function are influenced by the choroid plexus, whose dynamic cellular and transcriptional changes shape immune cell trafficking and cerebrospinal fluid composition. Here, we performed a comprehensive multi-omics analysis—including bulk and single-cell transcriptomics and epigenomics—of the lateral ventricle choroid plexus across postnatal and adult stages in mice and rats. We identified changes in the choroid plexus cellular composition and gene expression profiles, including early and progressive activation of several immune related genes in main cell types from early postnatal to young adult stage. Epithelial cells exhibited developmental remodeling over time, characterized by distinct gene expression programs, locus-specific changes in chromatin accessibility, and cellular diversity. In addition, we uncovered an epithelial cell population characterized by a distinct transcriptional signature. Our study offers a comprehensive atlas of transcriptional activity and chromatin accessibility in choroid plexus cells, providing a valuable resource to guide future research.

title: Organization of retrosplenial cortex projections at the single-neuron level
abstract: The retrosplenial cortex (RSP) supports spatial cognition, memory, and brain-wide information integration, yet its output architecture remains poorly resolved at single-neuron resolution. Using fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST), we reconstruct sparsely labeled neurons sampled predominantly from the anterior RSP across the whole brain. We find three major projection routes-cortical-restricted (CR), thalamic-restricted (TR), and thalamic-brainstem collateral (TBC)-and classify neurons into ten projection subtypes with distinct target-selective profiles. Somatic location and volumetric features are associated with axonal projection patterns. TR-pattern neurons show subregion-dependent thalamic targeting, whereas TBC-pattern neurons display greater axonal complexity and subtype-specific collateralization toward thalamic, midbrain, and hindbrain targets. Bilaterally projecting neurons across distinct projection patterns show cross-network projection modes with an overall ipsilateral preference and laminar-specific commissural architectures. Together, these findings provide a single-neuron anatomical map of RSP cortical, thalamic, and cortico-subcortical output patterns and a framework for examining distributed information processing across brain-wide networks.

title: Pharmacological blockade of p65 palmitoylation modulates NF-κB transcriptional activity
abstract: Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) regulates inflammation and immunity and is frequently dysregulated in autoimmune diseases, inflammatory disorders, and cancers. Cytokines and pathogens activate NF-κB transcription factors, and nutrients and metabolites, including fatty acids, also modulate its activation, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we report that RelA (p65), a major component of the NF-κB transcription complex, is autopalmitoylated at cysteine 197 and 206. Palmitoylation of p65 enhances its nuclear localization and p65-p50 complex formation, thereby increasing NF-κB transcriptional activities. We further show that licochalcone D, a small-molecule anti-inflammatory compound, directly inhibits RelA/p65 autopalmitoylation, suggesting it may act through an additional mechanism. These results indicate that fatty acid metabolism can directly regulate NF-κB activity through p65 palmitoylation and suggest that targeting p65 autopalmitoylation may be a therapeutic strategy for diseases with dysregulated NF-κB signaling.

title: LSR targets YAP to modulate intestinal Paneth cell differentiation
BATF condensation drives gastric cancer metastasis via chromatin association and transcriptional regulation
abstract: While liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is understood to be relevant with various types of cancers, the relationship between LLPS and gastric cancer (GC) remains ambiguous. In this study, we demonstrate that the basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor (BATF) shows increased DNA-binding activity and expression in GC tissues and cell lines, based on assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATAC-seq) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analyses. Additionally, in GC cells, BATF forms droplet-like nuclear condensates. Using combined approaches of chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq), ATAC-seq, and RNA-seq, we find that BATF condensation promotes its binding to the TM4SF1 promoter and enhancer regions, thereby regulating TM4SF1 transcription and prompting the TM4SF1-driven formation of focal adhesions and GC metastasis. Thus, we unveil a role for BATF LLPS in GC metastasis through its modulation of chromatin association and transcriptional regulation, highlighting the relevance of LLPS to GC progression and potential treatment approaches.

title: Optogenetic reduction of theta oscillations induces remapping of time cells without memory impairment
abstract: In a delayed alternation spatial working memory task, hippocampal time cells fire during specific moments of the delay period to form a sequential representation of the entire delay interval. The causal relationship between these sequences and working memory remains unclear. Similarly, hippocampal theta oscillations are thought to support working memory, primarily through the generation of time cell sequences. To causally examine these relationships, we optogenetically silence the medial septal GABAergic theta-generating circuit during the delay portion of a delayed spatial alternation task. With hippocampal theta oscillations substantially reduced, many time cells exhibit remapping, and new time cells are recruited. Despite partial remapping of time cell sequences, behavioral performance remains intact and trajectory-specific coding is preserved, suggesting that task-relevant information remains available under theta disruption.

title: Interaction of Discoidin Domain Receptor 1 with a 14-3-3-Beclin-1-Akt1 Complex Modulates Glioblastoma Therapy Sensitivity
Structural remodeling and activation of the hdeAB and proVWX operons in response to pH and salt stress
abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. The histone-like nucleoid structuring protein H-NS is an NAP acting as a global regulator of stress genes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. To investigate the regulatory interplay between these two proteins, we examined transcription, DNA binding, and chromatin structure at two regulated operons, hdeAB and proVWX, in E. coli following exposure to acid and salt shock. Our results show that H-NS senses pH and osmotic cues to remodel chromatin and relieve repression, while StpA-in part-compensates for H-NS loss, particularly at proVWX, highlighting a coordinated regulatory network.

title: Programmed DNA breaks drive chromatin reconfiguration and facilitate transcriptional potentiation at neuronal early response genes
abstract: Neuronal activity causes topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4. TOP2B-mediated DSBs facilitate ERG transcription, yet how this occurs is unclear. Using circular chromosome conformation capture (4C-seq), we report here that DSB formation is sufficient to emulate contact profiles observed at the promoters of Fos and Npas4 following neuronal stimulation, including elevated interactions with their cognate enhancers. Despite their purported risk, recurrent DSB cycles progressively potentiate ERG induction in mouse cortical neurons and HEK293T cells, evoking the effects of transcriptional memory. Potentiated ERG inducibility following recurrent DSBs persists through intervening cell cycles, occurs even when DNA repair is likely mutagenic, and correlates with a substantial loss of cis- and a gain of trans-, chromosomal interactions with ERG promoters. Together, these results reveal how activity-induced DSBs impact transcription by regulating chromatin dynamics at ERG promoters.

title: TIA1 is required for microglial activation in tauopathy
abstract: The RNA-binding protein T cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA1) regulates cellular stress responses and tau pathology, key contributors to the pathophysiology of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). TIA1 acts in peripheral monocytes to inhibit inflammation, but its function in central microglia, critical to neuroinflammation and disease progression, remains unknown. Here, we crossed TIA1 microglial conditional knockout (cKO) mice (using a Cx3cr1-driven Cre element) with the PS19 P301S MAPT mouse model of tauopathy and demonstrated that TIA1 promotes microglial activation, with a corresponding suppression of microglia activation upon TIA1cKO. We observe striking reductions in cytokine (Tnf-α and Il-1β) and sensome markers (Clec7a, Trem2, and Itgax); importantly, these reductions were accompanied by decreases in tau pathology. Proteomic analyses show TIA1 interaction with the microglial proteins C1Q, previously implicated in microglial activation. These results position TIA1 as a regulator of neuroinflammation and tauopathy in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells, including microglia, with potentially divergent functions in central versus peripheral immune compartments.

title: Depletion of CARM1 slows in vivo tumorigenicity and rewires developmental programming in glioma stem-like cells
Proline transporters coordinate immune activation and regenerative capacity after injury in plants
abstract: A robust immune response and regenerative capacity are both essential for survival after injury. In plants, salicylic acid (SA) is essential for activating immunity but simultaneously suppresses regenerative capacity. The mechanisms coordinating the trade-off between immunity and regeneration remain poorly understood. Here, we identify proline transporters as key regulators of this balance. Mutations in two wound-induced proline transporters, ProT2 and ProT3, rescued exogenous proline-induced suppression of de novo root regeneration (DNRR) and enhanced DNRR. ProTs are required for SA-mediated suppression of regeneration, without affecting SA-dependent defense responses. Mechanistically, a ProT3-CPK1 complex modulates the dynamics of wound-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS), sustaining a ROS level that restricts DNRR after wounding. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of proline transport rescued SA-mediated suppression of regeneration and enhanced regeneration across multiple plant species. These findings establish proline transporter as a regulatory hub integrating stress-induced proline metabolism, SA signaling, and ROS homeostasis to balance immunity and regeneration, and highlight chemical inhibition of proline transport as a strategy to improve crop regeneration under biotic stresses without compromising disease resistance.

title: RIF1 coordinates the stepwise post-replicative H3K9me3 recovery
abstract: DNA replication causes the dilution of parental histones along with their specific post-translational modifications. The kinetics of restoring these marks on newly incorporated histones dictate how quickly genomic domains regain their epigenetic identity after replication. H3K9me3 is restored extremely slowly; the process of reconstitution, to achieve the pre-replication levels, continues throughout the following G1 phase. The molecular mechanisms behind this slow reconstitution are unknown. We show here that RIF1's reassociation with heterochromatin during mitotic exit is required to set up a chromatin environment permissive for histone methyltransferases to resume H3K9me3 deposition. RIF1 facilitates the recruitment of SUV39H1, HP1α and HP1β and is required for the increased tri-methylation of H3K9 that occurs during G1 phase. RIF1 is also indispensable for recruiting Protein Phosphatase 1α (PP1α) to heterochromatin, and the interaction between RIF1 and PP1α is essential for the maintenance of H3K9me3 levels. In addition, RIF1-PP1 complex temporally restrains the activity of Aurora kinase at heterochromatin, ensuring that phosphorylation of H3S10 does not precede replication. This creates a time- window permissive for SUV39Hs to initiate the reinstatement of H3K9me3.

title: ALKBH8 promotes acute myeloid leukemia progression by coupling codon-dependent translation elongation to mRNA stability
abstract: Background: Dysregulated mRNA translation is a critical driver of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression. However, the mechanisms governing translation elongation during AML progression remain to be elucidated. Here, we aimed to study the role and mechanism of tRNA-U34 methyltransferase ALKBH8 in regulating translation elongation in AML.Methods: ALKBH8 expression levels were analyzed using several independent datasets. Immunoblotting and quantitative polymerase chain reaction were used to evaluate the expression levels of ALKBH8 and other molecules. Knockdown and overexpression were used to evaluate the impact of ALKBH8 on leukemogenic potential in cultured cells, xenografts, and MLL-AF9-driven AML mouse models. Ribosome profiling, RNA sequencing, and tRNA modification analyses were used to determine the effects of ALKBH8 on mRNA translation elongation. Findings: ALKBH8 was found to be overexpressed in AML and correlated with poor patient prognosis. Genetic depletion of ALKBH8 markedly impaired the proliferation and leukemogenic capacity of AML cells both in vitro and in vivo. ALKBH8 mediates the mcm5U modification of tRNAs, facilitating efficient translation elongation. Loss of ALKBH8 induces ribosome pausing and preferentially destabilizes transcripts enriched in adenine-ending codons. ALKBH8 regulates the expression of DNA repair gene BRCA1 in a codon-dependent manner. ALKBH8 depletion sensitizes AML cells to the PARP inhibitor olaparib both in vitro and in vivo. Interpretation: Our study reveals a codon-specific mechanism by which ALKBH8 regulates oncogenic translation in AML and highlights the ALKBH8-BRCA1 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

title: AREG mediates transient hepatocellular carcinoma resistance to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors
abstract: Lenvatinib is a first-line therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Emerging studies suggest resistance evolves through dynamic multi-step processes. Here, using multi-timepoint and multi-omics sampling, we characterized the trajectory of lenvatinib resistance in HCC cells and identified three adaptive states marked by state transitions. Multi-omics analyses and functional validation identified amphiregulin (AREG) as a key transient mediator of resistance in our models. AREG is a sufficient and dominant ligand to promote cell survival through epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activation. Pharmacological inhibition of the AREG-EGFR axis specifically targeted early-resistant cells. Furthermore, AREG upregulation was validated in additional replicate experiments and another HCC cell line. Mechanistically, a focal deletion on chromosome 3p may contribute to NF-κB activation and AREG expression. This study delineates a recurrent yet transient adaptive mechanism and suggests new therapeutic opportunities-such as combination therapies targeting transient resistance mechanisms-to prevent or overcome drug resistance.

title: Dopamine signaling in the medial accumbens shell constrains the duration of reinforced actions
