abstract: Dopamine regulates the frequency of motor actions, but it is unclear whether it similarly regulates the duration of discrete behaviors. Here, we show that dopamine signaling within the medial accumbens shell reinforces actions while simultaneously constraining their duration. When mice hold down a lever to continuously self-stimulate dopamine axons in the medial accumbens shell, hold-downs are rarely longer than 5 s, and higher stimulation frequencies elicit shorter, but more numerous, lever hold-downs. This disengaging property of medial accumbens shell dopamine also applies to consummatory behavior, as mice are quicker to both terminate and reinitiate bouts of licking paired with high-frequency dopamine axon stimulation. Dopamine D1 receptors underpin this disengaging property of dopamine signaling, as we demonstrate a D1 agonist shortens both self-stimulation hold-downs and bouts of consummatory behavior. Altogether, we uncover an anatomically defined role of dopamine, which is to disengage its own reinforcing properties through D1 receptor signaling.

title: Hexokinase-2 moonlights as a suppressor of STING-mediated innate immunity
abstract: Metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized for "moonlighting" functions beyond their primary metabolic roles. While such non-canonical activities are well characterized in cancer biology, their roles in innate immunity remain poorly defined. Here, we show that Hexokinase II (HK2), a rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, suppresses STING-mediated innate immune responses independently of its enzymatic activity. Upon STING activation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) trigger the dissociation of HK2 from the mitochondria to the cytosol. Cytosolic HK2 then interacts with STING, impeding its oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi apparatus, thereby dampening downstream immune signaling. Notably, HK-TAT, a peptide that induces HK2 release from the mitochondria, effectively inhibits STING-dependent immune activation and ameliorates disease phenotypes in STING-driven autoimmune mouse models. Our findings highlight the moonlighting role of HK2 as a negative regulator of STING signaling and provide a potential therapeutic approach for treating autoimmune diseases driven by STING dysregulation.

title: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing in ischemic cardiomyopathy reveals common transcriptional profile underlying end-stage heart failure
Cryo-EM and biochemical characterization of a BRAF/CRAF heterodimer shows that the NtA motif negative charge is dispensable for RAF activation
abstract: Upon RAS-driven membrane recruitment, RAF kinases ARAF, BRAF and CRAF are activated via formation of homo- or hetero- dimers to initiate signaling through the MAP kinase cascade. Although RAF heterodimers are important for both physiologic and oncogenic signaling, they have been little studied at a structural and biochemical level. Here we report the preparation, biochemical characterization, and the cryo-EM structure of a 14-3-3-bound BRAF/CRAF heterodimer complex. The heterodimer exhibited kinetic parameters and sensitivity to a panel of twelve structurally diverse RAF inhibitors that were closely similar to, or intermediate between, those of BRAF and CRAF homodimers. Cryo-EM structures of the heterodimer with and without MEK1 revealed an overall organization essentially identical to that of RAF homodimers, but with an asymmetric interaction in the MEK1-bound structure in which the BRAF N-terminal acidic (NtA) motif extends across the dimer interface to engage the CRAF RKTR motif. Mutagenesis of this interface unexpectedly revealed that replacing the acidic NtA sequence with a basic RARA sequence yields highly active RAF homodimers and heterodimers, demonstrating that negative charge in the NtA motif is not required for activity. Collectively, our findings suggest that the charge state of the NtA motif influences RAF activity through effects on local backbone dynamics and the stability of the inactive kinase conformation, rather than via stereospecific recognition across the dimer interface.

title: Infection history and TCR sequence features shape the breadth of TCR cross-reactivity
abstract: The T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire enables recognition of a vast array of pathogens, despite containing far fewer unique TCRs than the diversity of encountered epitopes. This potential contradiction is resolved by TCR cross-reactivity, whereby individual TCRs recognize multiple distinct epitopes. However, the features defining broadly cross-reactive TCRs remain poorly understood. Here we systematically analyze TCRs from mice sequentially infected with influenza viruses containing naturally occurring single amino acid variants of the D b NP 366 epitope. We identify 967 unique paired TCR sequences across 18 infection histories and test 22 representative TCRs against 172 epitope variants, yielding 3,784 TCR-epitope interaction measurements. These TCRs exhibit a continuum of cross-reactivity, with infection history influencing both TCR sequence similarity and reactivity profiles. We find specific TCR sequence features associated with broader cross-reactivity, highlighting the interplay between epitope exposure, TCR diversity, and function, and providing insights into CD8 + T cell adaptability, immune memory, and vaccine design.

title: E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 activates the DNA damage response during papillomavirus life cycles
abstract: The papillomavirus life cycle is intricately linked to epithelial differentiation, and the virus manipulates the differentiation process to facilitate viral production. One such manipulation is activation of the DNA damage response (DDR) which promotes viral replication via homologous recombination. This report demonstrates that the papillomavirus transcription/replication/segregation factor E2 activates the DNA damage response (DDR). During differentiation, E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 causes CIP2A to bind and inhibit PP2A resulting in DDR activation via ATM phosphorylation. The DDR promotes inhibitory interaction of DBC1 with the class III deacetylase SIRT1, which further boosts the DDR via increased acetylation and stability of viral and host proteins. E2 forms a complex with TOPBP1 and ATM, while preventing ATR activation by blocking TOPBP1-ATR interaction. This "ATM up ATR down" phenotype promotes viral replication via ATM promotion of homologous recombination, and cell proliferation via inhibition of ATR. We demonstrate this mechanism of DDR activation in multiple systems: keratinocytes expressing only E2, in foreskin keratinocytes immortalized by HPV16, in HPV16 positive keratinocytes derived from a cervical lesion, in pre-neoplastic lesions induced by mouse papillomavirus MmuPV1, in head and neck cancer cell lines that retain E2 expression, and in HPV16 positive oropharyngeal patient derived xenografts that retain E2 expression. ATM inhibition preferentially killed cells expressing E2, presenting a novel strategy for treating HPV early preneoplasia and a large subset of HPV+ oropharyngeal cancers retaining E2 expression and episomal genomes.

title: BCLAF1 and responses to RAG-induced DNA breaks enforce pre-B cell checkpoint
abstract: During early B cell development, pre-B cells encounter signaling from pre-B cell receptor (pre-BCR) and DNA damage responses (DDR) triggered by RAG-induced DNA double-stranded breaks (DSBs) generated during immunoglobulin light chain (Igl) recombination. These signals drive cooperative and antagonistic programs to promote pre-B cell checkpoint. Here, we show in vivo that pre-B cells transition between distinct subpopulations predominated by either pre-BCR or RAG DSB-induced DDR signals. DDR initiates early in pre-B cells undergoing Igl recombination then drives cellular programming during terminal pre-B stages. We find that RAG DSB-induced DDR regulates coordinated pre-B cell differentiation, in part, by activation of the transcriptional repressor complex SPIC/BCLAF1. Loss of BCLAF1 disrupts pre-B cell developmental progression resulting in concomitant expression of pre-BCR and DDR programs with breakdown in segregation of clonal expansion and Igl recombination. These studies show that RAG DSB-induced DDR and BCLAF1 preserve pre-B cell checkpoint integrity in vivo during Igl recombination.

title: UFSP2 constitutes a targetable vulnerability via deUFMylation-dependent activation of AKT oncogenic signaling
abstract: AKT hyperactivation is a hallmark of many human cancers and contributes to poor clinical outcomes, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that AKT undergoes UFMylation, and loss of AKT UFMylation promotes colorectal tumor development and confers resistance to the AKT inhibitor AZD5363 (capivasertib). Furthermore, p53 activates ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) during the cell cycle to inhibit AKT activity. Conversely, AKT phosphorylates UFM1 to reduce its own UFMylation, establishing a feedback loop that sustains AKT activity. Moreover, we provide evidence that UFSP2 functions as a major cellular deUFMylase for AKT, and genetic ablation or inhibition of UFSP2 suppresses AKT activity to retard tumorigenesis in vivo. Together, these findings provide a mechanistic framework for UFMylation-dependent AKT regulation and support further investigation of UFSP2 inhibition as a potential strategy to modulate AKT signaling in colorectal cancer.

title: Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations
abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Sustained exogenous D-lactate did not abolish protection, placing D-lactate as a tractable readout of ecological restoration rather than its effector. Responsiveness is encoded in the baseline microbiota and predictable before intervention, establishing probiotic efficacy as a stratifiable property of the host microbiome.

title: RAStoERK: A reference interaction atlas for insights into signaling and disease
abstract: Summary The RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK pathway has been extensively studied for its roles in physiology and disease, yet a systems-level view of its interplay with the broader cellular context is lacking, limiting insight into paralog-specific roles, mutation-driven rewiring, and cross-pathway integration. To address this, we simultaneously mapped the interactomes of all pathway components and their activating and inactivating mutations, identifying 2,500 high-confidence interactors, 88% of which previously unreported, and generating a high-confidence, comprehensive reference map of the pathway in resting and activated states. The pathway behaves like a “molecular organism” that connects to other signaling complexes, operates from distinct subcellular sites, and integrates into networks relevant to physiology and disease. Dataset exploration uncovered paralog- and mutation-specific interaction signatures and pathway-level crosstalk, including previously unknown connections to mRNA metabolism and WNT signaling. The interactomes available at RAStoERK.univie.ac.at provide a foundational community resource for unbiased discovery, targeted mechanistic studies, and potential therapeutic exploration. Highlights High-resolution interactome map of the RAS to ERK pathway in resting and active states State-dependent pathway-level interactions with signaling and functional modules Mutation-driven interactome rewiring and integration into pathophysiological networks A resource to discover pathway crosstalk, disease links, and actionable interventions

title: Mechanisms of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline
abstract: Amphetamine-type stimulants (ATSs) disrupt the brain monoaminergic system and strongly stimulate motivation, movement, and addiction. Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) plays a vital role in monoaminergic neurotransmission by sequestering monoamines in presynaptic vesicles. How ATS binds to and regulates VMAT2 remains elusive. Here, we report the cryo-EM structures of human VMAT2 in complex with four ATSs (AMPH, METH, MDMA, and MDA) and the inhibitor lobeline, revealing the molecular mechanisms underlying ATS recognition and modulation. ATSs mimic monoamines and occupy the substrate-binding site of VMAT2, indicating that ATSs function as substrates and thus redistribute the vesicular monoamine pools to the cytosolic pools. Lobeline adopts an unexpected dual-binding mode and locks VMAT2 in a lumen-facing conformation, inhibiting monoamine and ATS uptake. Our dopamine release assay revealed that lobeline regulates AMPH-induced dopamine release by modulating both VMAT2 and DAT. This study provides important mechanistic insights into VMAT2 modulation by amphetamines and lobeline.

title: Embryonic reprogramming drives anaplastic transformation in thyroid carcinoma
abstract: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is a highly aggressive malignancy that often arises through anaplastic transformation of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Although genetic drivers such as BRAF and TP53 mutations are implicated, the mechanisms underlying this transition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that human ATC loses thyroid differentiation and acquires pluripotency-associated features, accompanied by MAPK pathway activation. Guided by parallels with induced pluripotent stem cell reprogramming, we develop an in vivo reprogramming mouse model. Forced expression of Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (OSKM) induces anaplastic transformation of Braf-mutant thyroid epithelium even without Trp53 mutation, yielding an ATC-like phenotype that shares molecular and histological features with human ATC. A conventional Braf/Trp53-mutant model shows similar features. Reintroduction of NKX2-1 into human and murine ATC cells partially reverses embryonic reprogramming, suppresses proliferation and induces redifferentiation toward a PTC-like phenotype. Embryonic reprogramming is a central driver of anaplastic transformation and supports redifferentiation strategies.

title: SIR2-mediated filament assembly activates the NLR-like protein Avs5 for bacterial antiviral defense
abstract: Like mammalian nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain receptors (NLRs), bacterial NLR-like proteins mediate antiviral defense. Avs5, a representative of a large family of short bacterial NLR-like proteins, contains an N-terminal SIR2 effector, a central nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), and a C-terminal sensor domain. Whereas canonical inflammasome NLRs use NBD oligomerization to nucleate effector-domain filaments, Avs5 forms SIR2-mediated filaments that couple receptor assembly to NADase activation. In the resting state, ATP-bound Avs5 is monomeric and subsequently forms a SIR2-mediated dimer that likely represents an intermediate in a stepwise activation pathway. Upon activation, ATP-dependent conformational remodeling of the NBD promotes conversion of these dimers into active filaments. Structure-guided mutagenesis, biochemical assays, and functional analyses show that filament assembly is required for efficient NAD + hydrolysis and antiphage defense. These findings reveal an effector-driven activation mechanism and extend the principles by which NLR proteins couple higher-order assembly to immune defense across domains of life.

title: Role of Leu and Val synthesis in sensing mitochondrial nutrient and energy availability
abstract: How cells integrate nutrient availability to coordinate metabolism and growth remains poorly understood. Here, we identify branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) synthesis as a metabolic sensing system linking mitochondrial activity to translational and transcriptional control. Yeast limits Leu and Val import and instead relies on their synthesis, allowing BCAA production to reflect mitochondrial anabolic capacity. Reduced Val synthesis activates Gcn2, whereas reduced Leu synthesis inhibits TORC1, together decreasing translation efficiency and restricting growth. This response lowers levels of the transcriptional repressor Mig1, suppressing the Warburg/Crabtree effect and promoting alternative carbon source utilization. Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of Leu/Val synthesis induces this metabolic reprogramming even in nutrient-rich medium, indicating that mitochondrial BCAA synthesis can partially override other nutrient-sensing pathways. Thus, BCAA synthesis couples mitochondrial anabolic capacity to Gcn2 and TORC1 activity and, through translational control of transcription factor abundance, shapes cellular metabolism.

title: Single-cell multi-omics reveals archetypal regulatory programs shared across T cell subsets
abstract: Abstract T cells protect against pathogens and tumors and can differentiate into various functionally distinct subsets. While each subset exhibits a characteristic epigenomic and transcriptional profile, essential immune functions such as self-renewal, expansion, cytokine production, and cytotoxicity are common to multiple subsets and therefore must be programmed via shared regulatory mechanisms. To uncover these regulatory “archetypes”, we integrated a new single-cell multiomic (scATAC+RNA-seq) dataset for CD4 and CD8 T cells responding to acute and chronic viral infection with a comprehensive compendium of bulk ATAC-seq data. Our analysis revealed that T cell identity is governed by a modular architecture, where distinct transcription factors drive the reuse of regulatory archetypes across T cell subsets and lineages. Notably, translationally important progenitor Tcf1 + CD8 T cells, critical for sustaining CD8 T cell responses and present in both acute and chronic infection, exhibited a composite regulatory state combining a CD8 T cell exhaustion program and, unexpectedly, a follicular helper CD4 T cell program. In sum, this resource will aid mechanistic dissection of adaptive immunity and immunotherapy design, and the framework will be broadly applicable across biological systems. Highlights – Single-cell multiomics and ATAC-seq atlas reveal T cell regulatory archetypes – A unified progenitor Tcf1 + CD8 T cell population is shared by acute and chronic infection – Progenitor CD8 T cell identity combines CD8 exhaustion and CD4 Tfh regulatory programs – A Tfh-like differentiation gradient underlies heterogeneity in progenitor CD8 T cells

title: CCN1-mediated stress signaling underlies intrinsic cardiomyocyte dysfunction in spinal muscular atrophy
abstract: Cardiac involvement in spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is increasingly recognized, but its cellular basis remains poorly defined. Using patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) and engineered heart tissues (EHTs), we identify reduced survival motor neuron (SMN) expression, mitochondrial respiratory defects, and impaired contractility in SMA. Transcriptomic analyses reveal cellular communication network factor 1 (CCN1) as a top upregulated gene in SMA iPSC-CMs, consistent with its enrichment in cardiomyocytes across cardiomyopathies. Exogenous CCN1 exacerbates contractile dysfunction in SMA iPSC-CMs. Proteomic profiling reveals sustained p38/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling activation, synergistically amplified by CCN1 and TNFα, thereby linking stress signaling to cardiac dysfunction in SMA. Therapeutic intervention with tanshinone IIA suppresses CCN1 expression, attenuates p38 activation, and improves contractile function. Notably, combining tanshinone IIA with risdiplam produces additive benefits in mitochondrial and contractile performance. Together, these findings identify a CCN1-mediated mechanism underlying SMA cardiac dysfunction and support combination strategies integrating SMN-dependent and independent therapies.

title: Early mitophagy defects and impaired mitochondrial energy metabolism drive target organ damage progression: Lessons from the Fabry heart
abstract: Abstract Increased literature support the pathogenetic role of dysfunctional energetic metabolism in the setup and progression of organ damage and failure. Genetic diseases often offer the possibility to investigate pathogenetic mechanisms. In particular, excessive cardiac damage is the most frequent cause of mortality in Fabry disease (FD), a genetic condition caused by deficient α-galactosidase A (GLA) activity, leading to globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation. Beyond Gb3 storage, metabolic alterations and mitochondrial dysfunction, supported by in vitro evidence or studies in other tissues, may contribute to FD cardiomyopathy. This study investigated, for the first time, the mechanisms of mitochondrial involvement in FD, its role in determining cardiac manifestations, and its potential as a therapeutic target. We used a humanized FD mouse model (R301Q-Tg/GLA knockout), along with derived embryonic fibroblasts and neonatal and adult cardiomyocytes, to assess mitochondrial function across the lifespan. FD cells showed impaired mitophagy, reduced mitochondrial respiration, and increased reactive oxygen species production. Importantly, this mitochondrial dysfunction exacerbated the lysosomal deficit in FD cells, forming a vicious cycle. In cardiomyocytes, these alterations progressed with age, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, energetic failure, and, in adult hearts, terminal mitochondrial damage and apoptosis. These events ultimately result in cardiac remodeling and dysfunction, including hypertrophy and diastolic impairment. Indeed, L-arginine supplementation, which promotes NO/PGC-1α–dependent mitochondrial rescue, prevented the development of cardiac abnormalities in FD mice. Our findings identify early mitochondrial dysfunction as a key driver of FD cardiomyopathy and support mitochondrial targeting, including L-arginine supplementation, as a promising adjuvant therapeutic strategy. The mechanistic link between lysosomal dysfunction, altered mitochondrial turnover, and energetic collapse emerges as a key targetable pathway in organ damage, extending beyond FD. Graphical abstract Cardiac manifestations vs mitochondrial alterations in Fabry disease: the visible tip and the hidden base of the iceberg Cardiac manifestations in hR301Q Tg/KO mice become evident from 9 months of age. However, mitochondrial homeostasis is perturbed much earlier (neonatal to young stages), with impaired mitophagy, reduced mitochondrial respiration and membrane potential, increased ROS production and PGC-1α downregulation. At later stages, from 6 months of age, mitochondrial dysfunction progresses and begins to impact cellular energetics, as indicated by reduced ETC expression and the onset of energetic deficit (ATP reduction). The resulting energetic collapse, together with progressive mitochondrial leakage, leads to cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, apoptosis, and dysfunction, which become detectable from 9 months of age, when clinical signs emerge. These findings support a mechanistic model in which 1) lysosomal incompetence due to GLA deficit is the initiating event inducing impairment of mitophagy; 2) Unsuccessful mitophagy, induces downregulation of PGC-1a-dependent mitogenesis; 3) exhausted mitochondria accumulate, inducing energetic collapse (able to exacerbate lysosomal dysfunction and further perturb mitophagy in a vitious cycle); 4) ultimate mitochondrial leakage induces Cytochrome C release and apoptosis activation. This cascade of molecular events is responsible for clinical manifestations, and mitochondrial targeting prevents cardiac organ damage. Significance statement Fabry disease is a rare genetic disorder in which cardiac complications are a major cause of death, yet underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify mitochondrial dysfunction as an early pathogenic event associated with impaired mitophagy, whereby defective mitochondrial quality control both results from and exacerbates lysosomal dysfunction, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that drives disease progression. Using a humanized model, we demonstrate that mitochondrial dysfunction is a key determinant of cardiac phenotype in vivo, driving energetic failure, oxidative stress, and cardiac damage. Importantly, L-arginine treatment restores mitochondrial function and prevents cardiac abnormalities. Our findings define a broadly relevant pathogenic axis linking lysosomal dysfunction, mitophagy failure, and mitochondrial impairment, that lead to impaired energetic metabolism and consequent cardiac hypertrophy, independently from GB3 accumulation. The implications of our study go beyond Fabry disease and support the therapeutic targeting of cellular energy homeostasis to prevent and treat organ damage and failure in chronic diseases. title: Heterogeneous contributions of APOBEC3 deaminases to substitution and indel mutagenesis in lung adenocarcinoma
abstract: APOBEC3 cytosine deaminases are major sources of cancer mutations. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), APOBEC3 activity drives tumor evolution and therapy resistance, nominating these enzymes as therapeutic targets. Although APOBEC3A drives most APOBEC3-associated mutational signature burden across cancers, the relative contributions of individual paralogs in LUAD remain unclear. Here, we define the roles of endogenously misregulated APOBEC3 deaminases using CRISPR-Cas9 knockouts and whole-genome sequencing of 197 long-term propagated single-cell clones. APOBEC3 mutagenesis falls into three patterns, driven predominantly by APOBEC3A, by both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, or minimal despite detectable enzyme expression. Commonly used surrogate measures, including mRNA and protein levels and in vitro deaminase activity, do not predict these contributions. We also provide the first causal evidence that endogenous APOBEC3A generates the indel signature InD9a, linking it to uracil excision following cytosine deamination. These heterogeneous contributions highlight the need for biomarkers that resolve individual APOBEC3 activities to guide therapeutic targeting.

title: The compositional encoding of hand-eye coordinated movements for single neurons in the posterior parietal cortex
abstract: Human posterior parietal cortex (PPC) is known to play a role in hand-eye (H-E) coordination, yet the underlying encoding mechanisms remain uncertain. We recorded 412 single neurons across 11 sessions from motor cortex (MC; n = 251) and PPC (n = 161) in a single human participant performing an H-E coordinated center-out task. While MC neurons showed negligible modulation by eye movements, 79% of PPC neurons had neural representations that were additively separable into independent hand- and eye-movement tuning curves. Due to this separability, representations could be separated and additively recomposed while maintaining structural similarity. Consequently, compositional decoders trained solely on single-effector movements could match the performance of decoders trained on coordinated H-E movements (hand: 66% vs. 69%; eye: 34% vs. 36%). These results show that, during simple center-out tasks, MC hand-movement codes are unaffected by eye movements and that compositionality can be used to modularly decode H-E coordinated movements in PPC.

title: Mesothelin-induced lysosomal biogenesis sustains neutrophil longevity to drive brain metastasis
abstract: Tumor-associated neutrophil (TAN) enrichment is a defining feature and driving force of brain metastases (BrMs), a leading cause of death in solid tumors. Yet, the mechanisms governing TAN enrichment in BrM remains undefined. Herein, we demonstrate that BrM cell-derived shed soluble mesothelin (sMSLN) critically prolongs neutrophil survival to facilitate tumor cell colonization and outgrowth in the brain. Specifically, sMSLN binds to toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) on neutrophil to activate the JAK2-STAT3 pathway. This activation promotes lysosomal biogenesis and function, reducing cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and inhibiting neutrophil apoptosis. Neutrophil depletion or TLR4-STAT3 blockade abrogates sMSLN-induced BrM progression. Targeting MSLN with Anetumab effectively reduces TAN enrichment, and combining this with TLR4 inhibition synergistically suppresses lung cancer BrM. Our findings establish a critical role for tumor cell-derived sMSLN in sustaining neutrophil longevity and driving BrM, highlighting the sMSLN-TLR4 axis as a promising therapeutic target for brain metastatic tumors.

title: One factor, two safeguards: RUNX1 divides its labor across the regulatory genome
abstract: Fritz et al. 1 1. Fritz, A.J. ∙ Greenyer, H. ∙ Dillac, L. ... RUNX1 links enhancer-centered control of epithelial identity with promoter-centered control of DNA-damage responsiveness.

title: PhIP-Seq reveals geography- and disease-associated human herpesvirus antibody repertoires and distinct EBV response modules
abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) has been implicated in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases, but herpesvirus-directed humoral responses across populations and disease states remain incompletely defined. We profiled antibodies to all nine human herpesviruses by PhIP-Seq in 908 serum samples from 848 individuals in Madagascar and Germany. Cohorts showed distinct reactivity patterns, including cross-virus associations between homologous alphaherpesvirus envelope glycoproteins. German cohorts recognized a broader range of latent and lytic EBV proteins than Malagasy controls, with increased reactivity in primary sclerosing cholangitis. Proteome-wide profiling detected reactivity to 60 of 79 EBV proteins; 29 contained at least one peptide recognized in >5% of participants. Co-occurrence analyses identified an EBNA2-EBNA3A/B/C module and BFRF3-EBNA1 and BZLF1-BMRF1 pairs in German cohorts. Peptide ELISA showed individual-level concordance with PhIP-Seq for EBNA1. These findings reveal geography- and disease-associated herpesvirus antibody repertoires incompletely captured by single-antigen serology.

title: Species-specific gene programs define divergent antiviral responses in Marburg virus reservoir bats and humans
abstract: Bats tolerate viruses that cause severe disease in humans. Egyptian rousette bats, the natural reservoirs of Marburg virus (MARV), sustain asymptomatic infection, whereas humans develop severe and fatal disease. To define the basis of this divergence, we establish a comparative framework using primary and immortalized Egyptian rousette and human cells exposed to double-stranded RNA and interferon (IFN). Bat cells upregulate antiviral effectors while limiting inflammatory amplifiers, a pattern further supported by analysis of independent in vivo MARV infection datasets. In contrast, human cells activate antiviral programs and immune hyperactivation in response to MARV. Integrating transcriptomic and proteomic analyses, we identify species-specific immune programs encompassing differential IFN-stimulated gene regulation, apoptotic control, and cytokine signaling. Our findings establish an integrative framework for understanding species-specific antiviral responses associated with MARV reservoir biology, identify pathways linked to immunopathogenesis in humans, and provide a foundation for future studies of host responses to filovirus infection.

title: Neuroprotectant development from small molecule inhibitors of CHOP/ATF4 expression
abstract: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease that is in urgent need of neuroprotective therapies. We previously revealed the critical role of neuronal endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress induced by optic nerve injury in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. We also demonstrated that modulation of the ATF4-CHOP branch of ER stress provides significant neuroprotection. Here, we present multiple new chemical series identified by high-throughput screening that inhibit ER stress-induced C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP) expression. We perform a structure-activity relationship analysis of one "hit" compound and establish two analogs with potent activities on inhibiting the expression of CHOP and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). We further demonstrate their neuroprotective efficacy in two optic neuropathy models; in both models, they increase survival of retinal ganglion cell somata and axons and preserve visual function. Together, this proof-of-concept evidence establishes the new ER stress modulators as promising candidates for further drug development to provide neuroprotective therapy for glaucoma and other optic neuropathies, and potentially for diverse CNS axonopathies.

title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams
abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Using activity-dependent tagging and sequencing, we profiled the DNA methylome and transcriptome of engram and non-engram nuclei from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after contextual fear conditioning with and without post-learning sleep deprivation. Fear learning induces coordinated CpG and CpH DNA methylation remodeling specifically in engram neurons, with each showing unique temporal dynamics, revealing CpH methylation as a separate component of the engram's epigenetic signature. Interestingly, sleep deprivation partially reverses learning-induced methylation changes and impairs memory recall, indicating that sleep supports engram-specific epigenetic consolidation. Integrating the engram methylome with single-cell transcriptome profiling, we construct a multi-omic molecular atlas of the BLA fear engram and identify Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target. BLA-wide and engram-specific Mid1 knockdown establishes its functional requirement for fear memory consolidation, providing an approach to identify behaviorally relevant epigenetic targets.

title: Stress hyperglycemia impairs FOXK2-dependent macrophage cardiac repair after myocardial infarction
abstract: Stress hyperglycemia (SHG) predicts poor outcomes after myocardial infarction (MI), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify FOXK2 as a key regulator of macrophage-mediated cardiac repair. FOXK2 expression was reduced in cardiac macrophages from hyperglycemic mice after MI and in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from patients with MI with SHG, whereas macrophage-specific FOXK2 deficiency aggravated cardiac injury. Under high-glucose conditions, FOXK2 was glycosylated at T552 by O-GlcNAc transferase, promoting its ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent degradation. Mass spectrometry and functional assays showed that the FOXK2 T552A variant resisted hyperglycemia-induced degradation. Integrated CUT&Tag and RNA-seq analyses revealed that FOXK2 restrained pro-inflammatory cytokine expression by suppressing H3K27 acetylation. Thus, our findings identify FOXK2 as a critical regulator that supports cardiac repair during hyperglycemia, and targeting excessive FOXK2 O-GlcNAcylation may offer a therapeutic strategy for patients with MI and SHG.

title: IFN-γ and proinflammatory cytokines induce astrocyte programs that support antigen-dependent CD4+ T cell restimulation
abstract: We report that type 2 interferon with proinflammatory cytokines induces astrocytes to express multiple components required for attraction of and antigen presentation to CD4+ T cells via MHC-II molecules. Re-analysis of astrocyte-enriched single-cell sequencing from bacterial mimetic-injected mice revealed a transcriptionally distinct interferon-responsive astrocyte population enriched for antigen-presentation-associated genes 24 hours after peripheral immune challenge. In vivo, we identify MHC-II+GFAP+ astrocytes localized to the surface of the brain across multiple mouse models of neuroinflammation and in human neurological disease tissue. In a pure in vitro culture system, astrocytes stimulated with IFNγ and proinflammatory cytokines express MHC-II, costimulatory molecules and lymphocyte-recruiting chemokines, and support rapid antigen-dependent expansion of previously activated CD4+ T cells. Using human iPSC-derived CNS cultures, we additionally show induction of antigen-presentation-associated machinery in human astrocytes following inflammatory cytokine stimulation. Rather than inferring function solely from marker expression, we assessed astrocyte-supported T cell restimulation in vitro and separately characterized the emergence of antigen-presentation-associated astrocytes in vivo at neuroimmune interfaces during inflammation in mice and humans. Together, these findings support a conserved role for cytokine-stimulated astrocytes in expressing antigen-presentation-associated machinery and, in vitro, supporting antigen-dependent restimulation/expansion of CD4+ T cells under inflammatory conditions.

title: Ataxin-2 loss flips a metabolic switch for neuron health
abstract: Gastaldo et al. 1 1. Gastaldo, D. ∙ Vito, S. ∙ Black, H.H. ... Ataxin-2 downregulation rewires neuronal and astrocytic metabolism to protect against TDP-43 toxicity Cell Rep. 2026; 45 , 118053 Full Text Full Text (PDF) Scopus (0) PubMed Google Scholar report that lowering ataxin-2 protects neurons from TDP-43 toxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis by activating neuronal glycolysis and astrocytic cholesterol synthesis, not by reversing TDP-43-dependent molecular pathology. The downstream effectors, IDH1 and HMGCS1, thus emerge as candidate therapeutic targets.

title: Dopamine turns mitochondrial stress into inflammation
abstract: Daniali et al. show that dopamine drives mitochondrial stress, mtDNA release, and cGAS-STING-dependent IL-6 production in human macrophages. These findings suggest a mechanism linking dopaminergic signaling to mtDNA damage signatures increasingly detected in blood from patients with Parkinson's disease.

title: Sense-and-respond: Engineered bacteria drive epithelial repair during gut inflammation
abstract: Zhao et al. 1 1. Zhao, Y. ∙ Sun, Y. ∙ Zhu, X. ... An engineered probiotic for diagnosis and mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel disease Cell Rep. 2026; 45 :118171 Full Text Full Text (PDF) Scopus (0) PubMed Google Scholar engineer a reactive oxygen species-responsive probiotic strain of Escherichia coli that senses intestinal inflammation and responds by locally delivering IL-22-Fc to promote epithelial repair, establishing an integrated sense-and-respond platform for inflammatory bowel disease diagnosis and mucosal healing.

title: Molecular insights into the activation mechanism of the slow anion channel AtSLAH3
abstract: The plant slow anion channel SLAH3 regulates essential physiological processes, including stomatal closure and stress responses, yet the structural mechanism underlying its activation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the activation mechanism of SLAH3 by determining cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the wild-type (WT) channel and gain-of-function mutants identified through a targeted mutagenesis screen of pore-lining residues. Notably, the L400A mutant was captured in a dilated, open-like conformation, in contrast to the auto-inhibited WT channel. Structural comparisons revealed concerted rearrangements of the pore-lining transmembrane helices and intracellular regulatory elements. The observations point to an activation model in which displacement of the intracellular auto-inhibitory module relieves pore occlusion, triggering conformational changes that propagate from the intracellular loop to pore-lining segments, ultimately widening the entrance for anion transport. Therefore, our study provides a structural framework for understanding SLAH3 regulation and advances our understanding of nitrate signaling and stress adaptation in plants.

title: A stress-adapted fiber state promotes clonal expansion of deleted mitochondrial DNA
abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion and multiple deletions frequently coexist in mitochondrial disease, neurodegeneration, and aging, yet how the two relate and why deletions accumulate focally remain unresolved. Here, longitudinal bulk and in situ analyses of Mpv17 −/− murine muscle reveal that a compensatory rise in mitochondrial transcripts per mtDNA initially offsets severe, uniform mtDNA depletion, preserving the respiratory chain. However, this response carries a delayed cost: by six months transcripts decline, mtDNA deletions emerge, and respiratory-deficient fibers appear. Paradoxically, fibers harboring deletions accumulate supra-physiological amounts of mtDNA, despite prior depletion. This expansion is invariably accompanied by elevated Hsp60, and the same holds in human mitochondrial myopathy. We propose that depletion reprograms mitochondrial DNA and RNA metabolism, inadvertently promoting deletion formation and creating an Hsp60-high fiber state permissive for clonal expansion. Therefore, depletion and multiple deletions can be sequential phases of a common degenerative process, relevant also to aging and neurodegeneration.

title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome FXR/Sptlc2 signaling promotes alveolar macrophage mitophagy and limits lung inflammation
abstract: Alveolar macrophages (AMs) undergo functional reprogramming that critically regulates lung inflammation. Although mitophagy is essential for mitochondrial quality control, its role in macrophage functional reprogramming during acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains unclear. Here, we identify the nuclear receptor Nr1h4 (FXR) as a transcriptional regulator of mitophagy in AMs. FXR activation transcriptionally upregulates serine palmitoyltransferase long chain base subunit 2 (Sptlc2), thereby enhancing mitophagy and promoting an anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype under inflammatory conditions. The FXR/Sptlc2 axis reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediator production while increasing anti-inflammatory markers. Conversely, FXR deficiency impairs mitophagy, exacerbates pulmonary inflammation, and aggravates lung injury in vivo. These findings establish the FXR/Sptlc2 axis as a regulator of mitochondrial quality control and macrophage functional reprogramming and identify it as a potential therapeutic target in ARDS.

title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes
abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

title: Locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons have diverse activity patterns across species and biological context
abstract: The locus coeruleus (LC) brainstem cell group is evolutionarily conserved across vertebrates and influences both mind (cognition) and body (cardiorespiratory, metabolic, and immune functions) via two-putatively distinct-spontaneous activity patterns. Yet, the degree to which spontaneous LC firing rates and patterns are homogeneous across species has never been assessed due to inherently limited sample sizes. To remedy this, we pooled cross-species data from 20 laboratories to show that firing rates differ across species and are modulated by sex, age, and type of in vitro or in vivo preparation. Contrary to the prevailing dual-mode firing pattern schema, we observed patterns spread across a low-dimensional manifold, with subregions enriched for specific biological factors and neurodegenerative disease models. Our findings show considerable diversity in an ancestral vertebrate neuromodulatory system.

title: CSE1L enrichment in pediatric and young adult acute myeloid leukemia reveals a ribosomal export dependency
abstract: Proteins shuttle between the nucleus and cytoplasm through the nuclear pore and via nuclear transport receptors, termed importins and exportins. Although genetic alterations involving nucleoporins are enriched in pediatric, adolescent, and young adult (AYA) acute myeloid leukemia (AML), nucleocytoplasmic transport has not been extensively studied in this disease. We discover that genes encoding nucleocytoplasmic transport pathway components (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes [KEGG]: hsa03013) are enriched in AML cells from younger patients (≤40 years). Within this pathway, CSE1L is the highest expressed exportin in pediatric/AYA AML and shows minimal expression in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). CSE1L depletion reduces leukemic cell growth, proliferation, and clonogenic capacity, targeting leukemia stem cells while sparing normal HSCs. Mechanistically, we identify a novel Ran-GTP-dependent role for CSE1L in regulating pre-60S ribosomal subunit export in AML. Collectively, these data identify nucleocytoplasmic transport and ribosomal subunit export as enriched dependencies in pediatric/AYA AML and establish CSE1L-mediated export as a leukemic vulnerability.

title: Antibody 3CF5 neutralizes historical and emerging H5Nx influenza viruses by targeting a conserved non-receptor-binding hemagglutinin epitope
abstract: Avian influenza viruses of the H5Nx subtype pose persistent pandemic threats. Here, we immunized rhesus macaques with an H5N6 vaccine and obtained 30 H5-reactive monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). Three IgG mAbs, 3CF5, 3BG3, and 3BE7, demonstrated potent neutralizing activity against multiple H5Nx viruses and conferred protection in a lethal mouse challenge model. Notably, 3CF5 exhibited broad neutralization against H5Nx viruses spanning 1997-2024, including contemporary clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 strains associated with an ongoing outbreak in dairy cattle. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analysis revealed that 3CF5 targets a conserved non-receptor-binding epitope on the hemagglutinin (HA) head, spanning the vestigial esterase domain and an adjacent lateral surface. 3CF5 mediates neutralization primarily through inhibiting membrane fusion and also possesses antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Furthermore, isotype conversion of 3CF5-IgG to mucosal secretory IgA1 (sIgA1) enhanced neutralization potency against H5N1 viruses up to 128-fold, highlighting the advantage of sIgA1 as a nasally administered prophylactic agent.

title: The complexity of cerebral small vessel disease: In search of the ideal mouse model
abstract: Currently, there are few animal models that reflect the physiological complexity of cerebral small vessel disease. Ruan et al. 1 1. Ruan, J. ∙ Nasrollahi, A. ∙ Martin, C. ... Loss of laminin-γ1 in pericytes impairs microvascular function and cognition Cell Rep. 2026; 45 , 117904 Full Text Full Text (PDF) Scopus (1) Google Scholar presented a pericyte-specific knockout of laminin-γ1 that exhibited several key disease-typical characteristic features at 11 months of age.

title: Influenza virus antagonizes self-sensing by RIG-I to enhance viral replication
abstract: Innate immune sensors must finely distinguish pathogens from the host to mount a response only during infection. RIG-I is a cytoplasmic sensor that triggers a broad antiviral response in response to sensing foreign RNAs. Here, we show that RIG-I not only binds viral RNAs but is activated by host RNAs. These are primarily non-coding RNAs transcribed by RNA polymerase III. They are benign under normal conditions but become immunogenic during influenza virus infection, where they signal via RIG-I to suppress viral replication. These RNAs are also bound by influenza virus nucleoprotein (NP), which normally functions to encapsidate the viral genome. NP interacts with RIG-I via an RNA bridge and antagonizes sensing of self-RNAs to counter innate immune responses. Overall, we demonstrate that self-sensing is strategically deployed by the cell to amplify the antiviral response and reveal a newly identified viral countermeasure that disrupts RIG-I activation by host RNAs.

title: Transcriptional and functional profiling reveals a dynamic continuum of beta-cell activation states
abstract: A central question is whether beta-cells respond uniformly to glucose. Using phospho-S6 as an activation marker, this study shows that beta-cells are recruited sequentially as glucose concentrations increase. Recruitment is spatially organized, with high-threshold cells predominantly located in the islet core. Transcriptomic profiling indicates functional heterogeneity among beta-cells. A low-threshold subset is characterized by enhanced stress resilience necessary for sustained secretion. An intermediate subset, enriched for calcium-signaling and vesicle-excitatory genes, modulates postprandial glucose excursions. The high-threshold subset specializes in high-capacity protein synthesis and insulin secretion to manage glucose peaks. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that these functional subsets form a continuous spectrum rather than discrete subpopulations. This division of labor is adaptable; under high-fat diet-induced metabolic demand, islets undergo remodeling with a global reduction in activation thresholds and a shift toward high-capacity profiles. Collectively, these findings identify a beta-cell hierarchy that balances metabolic resilience with secretory demand to maintain glucose homeostasis.

title: MHC II-expressing bone marrow megakaryocytes are noncanonical antigen-presenting cells and activate CD4+ T cells ex vivo
abstract: Abstract While professional antigen-presenting cells drive adaptive immunity, atypical cell types can fulfill this role in the bone marrow. Megakaryocytes (MKs) are canonically recognized for platelet production, but recent studies indicate functional heterogeneity and immune potential. We found that ∼20% of bone marrow MKs express Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) II and co-stimulatory receptors CD80, CD86, CD40, and CD83. These MKs process and present antigen to activate T cells ex vivo in an MHC II-dependent manner. MK/T cell interactions induced TGF-β1 secretion and promoted induced Treg differentiation. Prior stimulation of MKs with LPS or Poly I:C was associated with modest Th1-associated CD4+ T cell responses, including IFN-γ and TNF-α production, without robust Th17 differentiation. Immunopeptidomics of the murine MK MHC II receptor confirmed occupancy by exogenous peptides, suggesting in vivo functionality. Using a murine model with MK-targeted deletion of MHC II (Pf4-MHC Δ/Δ), we observed altered TLR signaling and reduced bone marrow TGF-β1. Together, these findings identify MHC II+ MKs as noncanonical antigen-presenting cells with the potential to modulate CD4 T cell responses as part of the immune regulation of the bone marrow niche.

title: Machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling reveals distinct transcription-dependent constraints on chromatin motion in living cells
abstract: Genomic DNA is wrapped around core histones to form nucleosomes, which are organized in cells from euchromatin to heterochromatin with distinct genome functions. Although transcription is known to shape chromatin behavior in live cells, it remains unclear how different transcription systems act across chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments. We develop machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling to classify euchromatin and heterochromatin classes (classes IA, IB, II, and III) and combine it with single-nucleosome imaging in living human cells. Nucleosome motion is progressively constrained from euchromatin to heterochromatin. RNA polymerase II inhibition by THZ1, DRB, or α-amanitin increases nucleosome motion in euchromatic classes IA and IB and in heterochromatin around nucleoli, but not at the nuclear periphery. In contrast, RNA polymerase I inhibition by CX-5461 selectively increases nucleosome motion in Class III heterochromatin around nucleoli. Our study reveals that Pol II and Pol I transcription shape chromatin behavior in distinct chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments.

title: Macrophages iron out cancer cells’ vulnerability
abstract: Surviving despite accumulating toxic metabolites inside the cell is a defining feature of cancer evolution. In the current issue of Cell Reports , Eric Cheung and coworkers identify a mechanism that enables the survival of malignant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cells through the sequestration of reactive iron. 1 1.
