title: Conserved disordered regions and ubiquitin-binding motifs within HUWE1 contribute to substrate targeting plasticity
abstract: E3 ligases confer substrate specificity within ubiquitin-dependent pathways. However, the pleiotropic HECT-type E3 ligase HUWE1 targets a biochemically and structurally diverse set of substrates through mechanisms that remain largely unknown. We develop a combinatorial cell-based system integrating global proteomics, proximity labeling, and reporter assays to systematically interrogate HUWE1 sequence features that enable substrate targeting. We define a robust HUWE1 activity signature consisting of putative substrates that accumulate upon HUWE1 impairment across multiple cell lines. By re-expressing a panel of HUWE1 deletion mutants, we find that both the largest intrinsically disordered region and the conserved ubiquitin-binding motifs contribute to substrate targeting. Structural modeling and domain analysis further suggest that HUWE1 achieves targeting plasticity through multivalent interactions, engaging both disordered and structured regions within its substrates. Together, our findings establish a framework for understanding how large, modular E3 ligases exploit intrinsic disorder and multivalency to shape their substrate repertoires.

title: A hyper-IgM2 AID mutation limits IgH break formation but preserves affinity maturation
abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) drives antibody diversification through class switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM). Humans with an AID mutation deleting the last nine amino acids (AID R190X ) develop hyper-IgM syndrome with defective CSR but variable SHM, suggesting that the C terminus plays a marked role in CSR. To model this putative separation-of-function mutation, we generated an Aicda R190X knock-in mouse. These mice show a severe CSR defect and a moderately reduced but ongoing SHM. Mechanistically, the severe CSR defect correlates with defective recombination of double-strand breaks in immunoglobulin switch regions. Strikingly, fusion of AID R190X to a catalytically inactive AID restores CSR, indicating that the C terminus mediates a non-catalytic function for recombination. This mouse model of the human R190X mutation demonstrates that the AID C terminus is indispensable for CSR and also contributes to efficient SHM, providing insight into the mechanistic basis of hyper-IgM immunodeficiency.

title: Rheb in central amygdala somatostatin neurons regulates chronic itch and anxiety-like behaviors
abstract: Chronic itch represents a significant clinical challenge that substantially impairs patients' quality of life, yet its underlying neural circuit and molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that somatostatin-expressing (SST) neurons in the central amygdala (CeA) are activated and functionally required in a mouse model of diphenylcyclopropenone (DCP)-induced chronic itch. Transcriptomic profiling further revealed upregulation of Ras homolog enriched in brain (Rheb) within DCP-TRAPed CeA SST neurons. Notably, Rheb knockdown suppressed the hyperexcitability of CeA SST neurons and alleviated chronic itch-related scratching and anxiety-like behaviors in DCP-treated mice. Conversely, Rheb overexpression promoted scratching and anxiety-like behaviors in naive mice. Collectively, these findings delineate a Rheb-regulated CeA SST neuronal mechanism that contributes to chronic itch-related scratching and anxiety-like behaviors, highlighting a potential molecular target for therapeutic intervention in chronic itch.

title: Clusterin, through exercise-mediated liver-heart crosstalk, promotes heart regeneration after myocardial infarction
abstract: Loss of cardiomyocytes drives cardiac remodeling and ultimately leads to heart failure, highlighting the need to promote cardiac regeneration. Exercise has been known to enhance cardiac repair and stimulate cardiomyocyte proliferation; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we demonstrated that exercise-induced exerkine clusterin mediates the pro-regenerative effects of running plasma on cardiac repair and cardiomyocyte proliferation following myocardial infarction (MI). Cardiac-specific Clu knockout attenuated, whereas clusterin overexpression enhanced, post-MI cardiac regeneration. Recombinant clusterin administration promoted heart regeneration in adult mice after MI. Mechanistically, clusterin activated NF-κB via proteasome-dependent IκBα degradation through direct binding with IκBα. Furthermore, the liver was identified as the major source of exercise-induced circulating clusterin; hepatocyte-specific Clu knockdown abolished the stimulatory effect of exercise plasma on cardiac regeneration. This study reveals a liver-heart crosstalk mechanism by which exercise-induced clusterin promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation, positioning clusterin as a potential therapeutic target for post-MI heart failure.

title: Pot1a maintains mesenchymal stem cell niche function to support hematopoietic stem cells
abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) maintain their function through interactions with niche cells in the bone marrow. We previously demonstrated that protection of telomeres 1a (Pot1a), a shelterin component, maintains HSCs and neuron-glial antigen 2-expressing (NG2 + ) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) by suppressing DNA damage response (DDR) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. However, the role of Pot1a in leptin receptor-expressing (LepR + ) MSCs, a primary HSC niche component, remains unclear. LepR-specific Pot1a knockout mice showed decreased LepR + MSC numbers, increased DDR and ROS production, reduced HSC quiescence, and impaired long-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, cell-permeable Pot1a enhanced the hematopoietic-supporting function of LepR + MSCs. Pot1a deficiency reduced pleiotrophin ( Ptn ) expression, whereas Pot1a overexpression increased its expression. These findings suggest that Pot1a preserves LepR + MSC function by limiting stress-associated changes, maintaining MSC numbers, and regulating hematopoietic-supportive factor expression, including PTN.

title: A competitive PDLIM1-USP14 axis destabilizes ACTN4 to disturb the invasive homeostasis of trophoblast in preeclampsia
abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by insufficient extravillous trophoblast (EVT) invasion, but the cytoskeletal mechanisms restraining EVT motility remain unclear. TMT-based placental proteomics identified the cytoskeletal adaptor PDLIM1 as markedly upregulated in PE. In primary trophoblasts and cell lines, PDLIM1 depletion remodeled the actin cytoskeleton and enhanced migration and invasion, whereas trophoblast-restricted Pdlim1 overexpression impaired trophoblast invasion and placental development in mice. Mechanistically, PDLIM1 bounds the rod domain of α-actinin-4 (ACTN4) and competitively displaced USP14, limiting ACTN4 deubiquitination and shifting ACTN4 toward RNF38-associated K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. Importantly, placenta-targeted chondroitin sulfate A-binding nanoparticles delivering Pdlim1 short hairpin RNA (shRNA) alleviated PE-like maternal and fetal phenotypes in mice. Collectively, these findings define a PDLIM1-USP14-ACTN4 proteostatic axis controlling trophoblast invasive homeostasis and identify PDLIM1 as a potential therapeutic target in PE.

title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages
abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.

title: Cysteine promotes islet α-cell glucagon secretion by limiting oxidative inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels
abstract: Cysteine serves as a robust α-cell secretagogue. While diabetes alters both plasma cysteine and glucagon levels, the mechanisms of α-cell cysteine action remain unclear. Here, we identified cysteine as a key regulator of islet glucagon secretion through redox control of α-cell electrical excitability. Short-term cysteine depletion markedly suppressed hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion from both human and mouse islets. Moreover, cysteine-depleted islets showed reduced hypoglycemia-stimulated α-cell calcium (Ca 2+ ) influx. Islet glucagon secretion and α-cell Ca 2+ influx rapidly normalized following cysteine restoration. Cysteine depletion also reduced α-cell voltage-gated sodium channel (Na V ) conductance and action potential amplitude. Importantly, reducing agents restored Na V currents and glucose control of α-cell Ca 2+ handling in islets without cysteine. Together, these findings identify reductive amplification of Na V channels as a key mechanism required for hypoglycemia-stimulated glucagon secretion, highlighting cysteine as a critical regulator of α-cell redox state, electrical excitability, and glucagon secretion.

title: A single-cell comprehensive atlas of leukemia and its microenvironment
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) remains highly lethal, with treatment failure and relapse driven by dynamic cellular states and evolving interactions within the leukemic ecosystem. In this study, we built a comprehensive atlas of leukemia and its microenvironment (CALM) by integrating single-cell profiling from 73 AML samples and 9 healthy donors, bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) from 87 newly diagnosed patients, and 4 paired bone marrow and peripheral blood single-cell data. All datasets were linked to clinical, cytogenetic, molecular, and treatment-response annotations. Immune analysis revealed diverse T cell distribution across disease status, where patients with persistent disease exhibited greater clonal expansion. Machine learning modeling on conventional T cells identified a T-cell signature pertinent to AML and outcomes, which were validated in two cohorts. CALM is a publicly accessible and interactive portal (calm.mdanderson.org) for exploring cellular compartments, cell-cell interactions, and longitudinal transcriptional and clonal dynamics to enable hypothesis generation, biomarker discovery, and target validation.

title: Exposure to immune stimuli augments alveolar macrophages to acquire neutrophil antimicrobial molecules to prevent bacterial pneumonia
abstract: The protective adaptation of innate immune defenses against respiratory pathogens has been linked to previous exposure to immune stimuli; however, the underlying mechanisms of these adaptations are not yet fully understood. Here, we show that pre-exposure to a low dose of non-specific immune stimuli or infection protects against subsequent lethal methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) challenge. This enhanced protection concurs with increased alveolar macrophages (AMs) resulting from a self-renewal process in the lungs. Importantly, these AMs are programmed to acquire neutrophil-released antimicrobial enzymes from the extracellular space to clear MRSA, prevent tissue damage, and rapidly restore lung homeostasis. AM function depends on differential gene expression, including expression of the efferocytosis receptor Mer proto-oncogene tyrosine kinase (MerTK) and the anti-apoptotic regulator Bcl-xL. Thus, our data highlight that AMs acquire neutrophil enzymes as an integral component of innate immune adaptation.

title: Circulating FABP4 promotes obesity-associated breast cancer lung metastasis through PIP2
abstract: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for increased incidence and mortality in multiple cancers, including breast cancer. However, the key molecular mechanisms linking obesity to breast cancer progression remain incompletely understood. In this study, using several high-fat diet-induced obesity models, we demonstrate that obesity promotes breast cancer lung metastasis through elevated levels of adipocyte-derived circulating FABP4. Mechanistically, circulating FABP4 directly binds to a subset of breast cancer cells via the membrane lipid PIP2. This FABP4/PIP2 interaction activates PKC signaling and enhances mitochondrial ROS production, driving cancer cell migration. Genetic deletion of FABP4, either globally or specifically in adipocytes, markedly reduces obesity-associated metastasis. Moreover, therapeutic targeting of circulating FABP4 using a distinctive neutralizing monoclonal antibody significantly suppresses breast cancer metastasis in multiple preclinical models. Together, these findings identify the FABP4/PIP2 axis as a key mechanism underlying obesity-driven breast cancer and highlight it as a promising therapeutic target for treating metastatic breast cancer.

title: Cell size asymmetry regulates neural stem cell proliferation and lineage expansion in the Drosophila brain
abstract: Abstract Asymmetrically dividing invertebrate and vertebrate stem cells can generate unequal sized sibling cells. However, the functional implications of cell size asymmetry (CSA) are underexplored. Here, we use Drosophila neural stem cells (NSCs) to investigate how changes in CSA impact NSC proliferation and cell fate decisions. Using live cell imaging, NSC lineage analysis, and gene expression profiling, we find that altering CSA increases the NSC pool but decreases lineage size and the number of differentiating progeny cells. Modeling CSA in silico with a volume-sensitivity and NSC self-inhibition model can recapitulate these findings. Gene expression profiling further revealed that the NSC growth regulator Imp and the G1-S cell cycle regulator CycE are upregulated in NSCs with altered CSA, providing a potential molecular link to the volume-sensitivity model. We propose that cell size and position regulate NSC proliferation and differential potential, impacting lineage progression and progeny cell differentiation in the developing Drosophila brain.

title: The enemy of my friend is … my friend? Host phage-microbiome symbiosis: An unexpected story of mutualism and betrayal
abstract: How does a host turn a beneficial symbiont into a nutrient source? In this issue of Cell Reports , Zhu et al. describe a novel symbiotic mechanism where an animal hijacks a prophage in its symbiont, which triggers lysis and nutrient release.

title: Terms and conditions apply: A cytokine cocktail licenses astrocyte antigen presentation
abstract: Whether astrocytes are fully competent antigen-presenting cells has been debated for over four decades. Fisher et al. show they are, but only conditionally: IFN-γ and microglial cytokines are jointly required, and stimulated astrocytes drive antigen-specific expansion of CD4 + T cells.

title: HRS dephosphorylation at membrane contact sites promotes sorting within multivesicular endosomes
abstract: Abstract HRS is a receptor tyrosine kinase substrate and component of the ESCRT machinery. It enables sorting of ubiquitylated cargo into multivesicular endosomes (MVEs) for lysosomal degradation but also functions in receptor recycling. We show that co-depletion of its ESCRT-0 binding partners, STAM1 and STAM2, recapitulates defects in EGF receptor (EGFR) sorting onto intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) but does not mirror the increased MVE size evident after HRS depletion. Using mutagenesis of the endogenous gene or introduction of APEX2-tagged HRS variants, we find that HRS Y329/334 phosphorylation is dispensable for EGFR sorting and MVE size control. AnnexinA1 mediates endosomal contact with the ER and promotes EGF-stimulated ILV formation. We show that reduced ILV formation on AnnexinA1 depletion is accompanied by increased HRS phosphorylation, likely through reduced HRS dephosphorylation by ER-localised PTP1B. Conversely, Y329/334 mutation renders ILV formation insensitive to AnnexinA1 depletion. Our data suggest that rapid HRS dephosphorylation at ER:MVE contacts promotes efficient ILV formation.

title: The DUF2439/RADIF domain of ZGRF1 is a RAD51 interactor and facilitator
abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are extremely toxic DNA lesions that can cause loss of genetic information and cell death if left unrepaired. During S and G2 phases of the cell cycle, DSBs can be repaired by homologous recombination (HR). The human zinc finger GRF-type containing 1 (ZGRF1) helicase and RAD54B translocase both promote HR. Here, we report that the DUF2439 domain, shared by ZGRF1 and RAD54B, interacts with RAD51 in vitro , and provides resistance to the DNA interstrand-crosslinking agent mitomycin C (MMC). Furthermore, the DUF2439 domain is necessary for recruitment of ZGRF1 to MMC-induced foci. Finally, we show synergistic roles for ZGRF1 and RAD54B in facilitating homology-directed repair of a defined DSB, consistent with the reduced survival of double-mutant cells after treatment with MMC or the PARP inhibitor talazoparib. Based on these results, we propose that the DUF2439 domain recruits ZGRF1 and RAD54B to DNA lesions, where they facilitate RAD51 function to promote HR.

title: Cell death in context: From mechanisms to interventions
abstract: When, how, and why cells die, and what happens when they survive, have profound consequences for development, immunity, and disease. To coincide with the Cell Press Symposium "Taking programmed cell death from mechanisms to interventions," we bring together perspectives from researchers across career stages and areas of cell death research. From emerging mechanisms and consequences of cell death to opportunities for therapeutic intervention, these voices highlight a rapidly evolving field and the questions that will shape its future.

title: Sex-biased enhancers shape transcriptional sex differences across human tissues
abstract: Sex differences influence human physiology and disease susceptibility, yet the regulatory mechanisms underlying sex-biased transcription remain unclear. Here we present eModule, which quantifies enhancer RNA (eRNA) transcription from Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) RNA-seq data to identify sex-biased active enhancers across 41 human tissues. We find that 47% of transcriptionally active enhancers are sex-biased in at least one tissue. These enhancers are tissue-specific, often organized into super-enhancers with chromatin signatures, and associated with rewiring of transcription factor (TF) regulatory networks. Evolutionary analyses reveal that many sex-biased enhancers are primate-specific and derived from transposable element (TE) exaptation, with contributing TE families enriched for binding sites of sex-associated TFs. Sex-biased enhancers also harbor variants linked to traits with sex differences and are inferred to regulate therapeutic target genes. Our findings position sex-biased enhancer activity as a regulatory layer shaping sex-biased transcription, with implications for regulatory evolution, GWAS interpretation, and sex-informed precision medicine.

title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice
abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LC DBH ) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LC DBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LC DBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LC DBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LC DBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

title: A hierarchical regulatory cascade programs chlamydospore formation in the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans
abstract: Chlamydospores provide durable stress tolerance for fungal survival and enable shelf-stable biocontrol agents, yet their genetic regulation in fungi remains poorly understood. Here, using the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys flagrans as a model, we define a hierarchical regulatory cascade for chlamydospore formation. LaeA mediates H3K9 monomethylation to license this developmental program. Furthermore, we identify VeA and Ste12 as LaeA partners, and the importin KapA as a nuclear gatekeeper. This upstream module activates VosA/VelB, which induces AbaA/StuA to control the effectors ChsG, McdD, and McdD-modified glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins for chlamydospore cell wall biogenesis. The expression levels of regulators within this regulatory cascade (LaeA/VeA/Ste12-VosA/VelB-StuA/AbaA-ChsG and McdD) determine chlamydospore yield and convert environmental cues into differentiation. This framework guides strain engineering for high-yield chlamydospore production and suggests a regulatory paradigm potentially conserved across fungi.

title: The YAP/TAZ-Tgfbr2-stiffness feedback loop governs divergent cell fates of muscle-resident mesenchymal progenitors
abstract: Mesenchymal progenitors are essential for muscle regeneration, but also contribute to fat accumulation and fibrosis. Several extrinsic and intrinsic factors regulating adipogenic or fibrogenic differentiation of mesenchymal progenitors have been identified, but it remains unclear how different cues are integrated to determine cell fate. Here, we demonstrate that interstitial stiffness and the mechanosensitive hippo pathway regulate mesenchymal progenitor cell fate. Fat accumulation model reduces interstitial stiffness and nuclear YAP/TAZ-positive mesenchymal progenitors compared to a regeneration model, whereas YAP/TAZ deficiency in mesenchymal progenitors enhances fat deposition. Mechanistically, YAP/TAZ directly induce expression of the anti-adipogenic genes Aldh1a2 and Wnt5a, and the pro-fibrogenic gene Tgfbr2, mediating TGF-β binding. Loss of Tgfbr2 in mesenchymal progenitors reduced transient collagen deposition, decreased stiffness, and increased fat accumulation during regeneration. We propose a stiffness–YAP/TAZ–Tgfbr2–collagen regulatory loop governing mesenchymal progenitor cell fate and highlight its importance for optimal muscle regeneration.

title: Exosome secretion is required for Sonic Hedgehog dispersal and signal gradient formation in the embryonic limb bud mesenchyme
abstract: Carrier-assisted diffusion and cytoneme transport help disperse Hedgehog morphogens across diverse embryonic tissues, yet their relative contributions to patterning mesenchymal tissues remain poorly understood. Here, we combine signaling assays with quantitative microscopy to establish exosome secretion as a major mechanism for Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) dispersal. Using a synchronous release system to visualize Shh trafficking, we demonstrate that Shh traffics through the exosome biogenesis pathway in limb bud mesenchymal cells. Shh-bound exosomes diffuse through extracellular space and also bind and travel along cytonemes, providing two alternative modes of transport. We show that exosome secretion is essential to establish short-range Shh signaling gradients in vitro and contributes to shaping Shh protein gradients in the limb bud in vivo . We propose that exosome-based Shh secretion, combined with different modes of extracellular transport, provides a tunable mechanism to sculpt Shh gradients across different length and time scales.

title: Programmed bacterial lysis in vivo alters host immune responses and microbial pathogenesis
abstract: Vibrio cholerae injects toxic type VI secretion system (T6SS) effectors to lyse sensitive intestinal commensals, but how this bacterial antagonism enhances mucosal host immune responses and its pathogenicity remains unknown. To mimic T6SS-mediated killing, we engineered V. cholerae lysis strains by using CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) to knockdown essential genes in peptidoglycan biogenesis or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport. Our results indicate that controlled bacterial lysis in vivo leads to divergent mucosal immune responses that directly modulate colonization and pathogenicity of a bystander, non-lysing V. cholerae ΔT6SS strain. Mass spectrometric analysis of the lysis debris revealed proinflammatory muropeptides correlating with these changes. We confirmed that oral co-administration of a synthetic peptidoglycan-derived metabolite with a V. cholerae ΔT6SS mutant, but not the wild type, shows dramatic enhancement of disease symptoms. These findings show that intestinal exposure to discrete bacterial cell wall metabolites can differentially modulate host innate immune responses and consequently bacterial pathogenesis.

title: A single-cell atlas of pediatric undifferentiated recurrent fever reveals candidate immune regulators
abstract: Children with periodic fever syndromes not attributable to infections, rheumatic disorders, malignancies, or known monogenic autoinflammatory conditions are classified as "syndrome of undifferentiated recurrent fever" (SURF). To date, treatment remains empirical, often resulting in only a partial response, underscoring the unmet clinical need for new therapeutic strategies. To advance the molecular understanding of SURF, we generated a large-scale single-cell RNA-seq immune atlas of 29 SURF patients with more than 200,000 cells. Comparison of patients with three healthy cohorts revealed large-scale metabolic shifts together with a distinct cytokine signature already observable during afebrile periods. This indicates that afebrile SURF cannot be considered a less inflammatory resting state but rather as a distinct homeostatic state. Furthermore, our analysis suggests an NAMPT-mediated autocrine feedback loop connecting the metabolic dysregulations with the pro-inflammatory phenotype in monocytes. This study offers insights into the SURF immunopathology and generates testable hypotheses to guide future therapies.

title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis
abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

title: eHLAstic reveals an extended canonical and non-canonical HLA-E immunopeptidome in human cancers
abstract: Human leukocyte antigen-E (HLA-E) is a non-classical MHC class I molecule with restricted polymorphism, offering a putative path to off-the-shelf therapies applicable across entire patient cohorts. Yet, the search for suitable cancer-restricted HLA-E targets has been hindered by low expression levels and limited knowledge on the wider HLA-E peptide repertoire, which is largely assumed restricted to a small set of canonical leader sequence-derived ligands. To address this, we developed eHLAstic, a dedicated HLA-E binding predictor, which improved the precision of HLA-E ligand discovery by almost threefold compared with existing approaches. Using eHLAstic and orthogonal biochemical binding validation, we identified and validated 31 previously unrecognised canonical and non-canonical HLA-E-associated peptides, including six cancer-restricted ligands detected in acute lymphoblastic and acute myeloid leukaemia but not in healthy blood or bone marrow cells. Many of the newly identified HLA-E ligands were shared across individuals with diverse HLA backgrounds. Moreover, most newly identified ligands were not confined to haematological malignancies but were also detected across multiple solid cancers. All but one of the non-canonical ligands were detected exclusively in cancer-associated samples and not in healthy cells or tissues. These findings redefine the HLA-E ligandome in healthy and cancer cells and uncover a previously unrecognized repertoire of canonical and non-canonical HLA-E ligands with potential for immune recognition and a promising route for therapeutic targeting.

title: Clearing perivascular light chain-derived amyloid to counteract aging-associated decline in liver regeneration
abstract: Aging impairs organ regeneration, with insufficient angiogenesis as a key contributor. Here, we show that the endothelial immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 is upregulated in aged mouse livers after partial hepatectomy. Endothelial PSMB8 deletion or PR-957 inhibition promotes angiogenesis and rescues liver regeneration. diGly proteomics identifies TAZ (transcriptional co-activator with PDZ-binding motif) as a ubiquitin-dependent immunoproteasome substrate, and TAZ activation restores aged liver regeneration. Aging triggers the infiltration of CD38 + IGLC1 + IgM B cells and aberrant perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition in the liver. Recombinant light chain-derived amyloid fibrils directly induce PSMB8 expression in vitro . Anselamimab-mediated light chain-derived amyloid clearance mitigates immunoproteasome overactivation and restores regeneration. Single-cell RNA sequencing confirms that anselamimab reverses aging-induced endothelial marker loss and inflammatory gene upregulation. Our findings establish a pathway linking perivascular light chain-derived amyloid deposition to regenerative decline via endothelial immunoproteasome activation, suggesting amyloid clearance as a promising therapeutic strategy for aging-associated decline in liver regeneration.

title: 5-Azacytidine incorporation into mRNAs disrupts translation and induces ribosome collisions
abstract: 5-Azacytidine (5-AzaC) is a cytidine analog and is widely used to treat myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Although its therapeutic activity is primarily attributed to hypomethylation resulting from DNA incorporation, the majority of 5-AzaC is incorporated into RNA. However, the functional consequences of 5-AzaC incorporation into RNA have been unknown. Here, we show that 5-AzaC treatment of cells leads to inhibition of protein synthesis. Ribo-seq, Disome-seq, and RNA-seq in cells treated with 5-AzaC exhibit a time-dependent C-to-G transversion signature in mRNAs within 2 h of treatment. These transversion events are enriched within footprint positions corresponding to the A-site of monosomes or leading stalled ribosome in a disome complex. Consistently, ribosome and disome footprints are accumulated at sites with C-rich codons in the A-site, specifically with the codons containing a C in the second position. 5-AzaC activates the integrated stress response (ISR) and the ribotoxic stress response (RSR) in a GCN2- and ZAK-dependent manner, consistent with disome-mediated signaling. Furthermore, loss of the Ribosome Quality Control (RQC) factor, ZNF598, sensitizes cells to 5-AzaC. Collectively, our results support a model where 5-AzaC is rapidly incorporated into mRNAs, disrupts decoding, and triggers disome-mediated signaling pathways, which contribute to its cytotoxicity. These findings suggest that translation disruption represents an additional layer of 5-AzaC's mechanism of action, alongside its known DNA-mediated effects.

title: Hyperosmotic stress induces rewiring of 3D chromatin interactions
abstract: Cells continually encounter environmental stressors that challenge homeostasis. How three-dimensional (3D) chromatin structure contributes to these stress responses, particularly under hyperosmotic conditions, remains poorly understood. Here, using time-resolved Hi-C, CUT&Tag, auxin-inducible depletion, and RNA-seq, we map 3D chromatin structure, its molecular drivers, and transcriptional outcomes during the hyperosmotic stress response. Within 1 hour of sorbitol treatment, pre-existing loops and domains undergo genome-wide collapse, accompanied by the emergence of several hundred de novo, sorbitol-induced loops that are more punctate, longer-range, and transient. These newly formed loops weaken over time and largely dissipate by 24 hours, coincident with recovery of pre-existing chromatin structure. Loop reorganization is consistent across human cell types and hyperosmotic stimuli. CUT&Tag and degron experiments reveal that sorbitol-induced loops require cohesin but not CTCF. Newly formed loop anchors are enriched at active promoters containing SP and KLF family motifs. Genes located at these anchors show little immediate transcriptional change but are activated several hours after loop formation, consistent with loops functioning upstream of gene activation. Together, our findings show that hyperosmotic stress triggers a rapid, reversible, and CTCF-independent reorganization of 3D chromatin interactions that helps coordinate transcriptional adaptation.

title: Plagl2 reprograms adult mouse retinal Müller glia for proliferation and injury-enhanced neurogenic competence
abstract: Summary Müller glia (MG) in the adult mammalian retina have long been recognized as a potential endogenous source for the regeneration of lost retinal neurons. However, existing MG reprogramming strategies yield an incomplete regenerative response by favoring either proliferation or neurogenic differentiation. Here, we show that the zinc-finger transcription factor Plagl2 , which has been demonstrated to rejuvenate aged neural stem cells, was sufficient to reprogram adult mouse MG into a progenitor-like state with coupled proliferative and neurogenic competence. Using histology, time-lapse imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics, we found that Plagl2 drove regulated rounds of MG cell cycle re-entry, while N-methyl-D-aspartate-induced retinal injury further promoted the acquisition of neurogenic competence toward inner nuclear layer neuronal identities. These findings identify Plagl2 as a novel rejuvenator of mammalian MG and support the general principle that reprogramming modules can be redeployed across cell types, offering new avenues for unlocking regenerative potential in otherwise non-regenerative tissues.

title: Temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte reprogramming
abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking asthma to lung cancer risk remains contradictory, presenting asthma as either a risk factor or a protective condition. We hypothesize that this heterogeneity stems from the temporal dynamics of inflammatory response and host genetic background. Using ovalbumin (OVA)-induced asthma models, we identify a temporal shift in immune effectors driving post-asthmatic tumorigenesis. During acute airway inflammation, eosinophil infiltration accelerates tumor growth across mouse strains. Following resolution, however, tumorigenic outcomes in recovery diverge along genetic lines. Prior asthma reshapes chromatin landscapes of bone marrow myeloid progenitors, establishing innate immune memory that differentially programs monocytes across strains. In C57BL/6 mice, trained monocytes adopt oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), acquiring a suppressive, tissue-remodeling phenotype that promotes tumor progression. Conversely, BALB/c-trained monocytes utilize glycolysis to maintain a pro-phagocytic state, enabling tumor clearance. These findings delineate a biphasic mechanism wherein temporal shifts in post-asthmatic immune responses define tumor outcomes via strain-specific monocyte metabolic reprogramming.

title: Single-cell and spatial characterization of the human pancreas in cystic fibrosis
abstract: Cystic fibrosis (CF) causes severely damaged pancreas morphology and results in high rates of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD), but the cellular pathways and regulatory programs driving CFRD pathogenesis in the pancreas are not understood. In this study, we performed single cell multiomic and spatial profiling of 2.04M cells in the pancreas from 23 non-disease and CF donors and defined regulatory programs and tissue niches of specific cell types and sub-types in CF. A high-mucin sub-type of ductal cells had relatively preserved abundance, altered localization and up-regulated stress, secretion and pro-fibrotic activity in CF, and conventional ductal cells showed evidence for transition to the high-mucin state. Increased inflammatory and fibrotic pathway activity in CF was linked to closer proximity and crosstalk between immune and stellate cells in specific niches. Beta cells had extensive genomic changes in CF, including increased stress and insulin secretion-related processes, and these changes were broadly distinct from those in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Islets in CF preferentially localized near large adipose tissue and collagen structures, and both areas were strongly linked to beta cell loss in CF due to signaling from adipocytes, macrophages, stellate, and high-mucin ductal cells. Overall, our results reveal cellular drivers of pancreatic dysfunction in CF and offer new in-roads to preserving beta cells in CFRD.
